item.title: A book lover's guide to the world's most literary hotels
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
I practically grew up in my local bookstore and worked there for more than a decade, so I’ve always loved the sense of calm that comes with being surrounded by books – that soothing yet enthralling feeling that entire worlds, eras, and rabbit holes are all within arm's reach. And there’s something extra irresistible about a hotel that leans into this literary escapism, boasting amenities like grand libraries stacked floor to ceiling with old-world volumes, sun-dappled reading rooms where you can lose an entire morning, and access to landscapes that once inspired the world's most famous authors. The bookish hotels on this list understand that pleasure, and turn reading into an essential part of the stay. Some have storied histories, with famous authors checking in as guests; others offer wonderfully over-the-top touches, from private libraries and book-filled suites to partnerships with local bookstores showcasing authors big and small. These are places built for lingering over a chapter with coffee, reading until the sun sets, and then reading some more – which, frankly, sounds like a pretty perfect way to travel, if you ask me. Read on for 11 of the best hotels for book lovers around the world, with properties from the Alps to upstate New York. FAQ: How we choose the best hotels for book lovers Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This is our top pick of hotels around the world for book lovers.

item.title: I needed 20+ years of address history. Gemini found it for me in minutes
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Filing out all the paperwork for a new apartment or home mortgage can be tough enough, but there’s one gotcha that can be particularly annoying: detailing the past addresses where you’ve lived over the past five, 10, or even 20 years, including dates for when you moved in and out. That tripped me up last year as I was completing a co-op application, leaving me to dig through my files for leases dating back a decade or longer. When did I move into that Brooklyn apartment on Henry Street, and what was the apartment number again? I got my address history ducks in a row eventually, but there’s an easier way to accomplish it—with the help of an AI agent. For this task, we’ll be using Gemini’s Spark agent and its Gmail connector. (Yes, you’ll need to allow Spark to comb through your Gmail inbox.) If you’re not comfortable with that, no problem—feel free to skip this tip. If you’re new to Gemini’s Gmail connector, see this article first for details about the best configuration settings and what you need to know about privacy. Once you have Spark’s Gmail connector configured, start a new thread and give it this prompt (which was crafted by Claude Opus 5.5): I need my address history for a form that asks where I’ve lived for the past [X] years. Search all of my Gmail, including archived mail, from [START YEAR] to today. 1. Look for anything that shows where I lived and when: leases and rental applications, move-in/move-out and security deposit emails, utility and internet start or stop services, USPS change-of-address confirmations, DMV or voter registration confirmations, mortgage or closing emails, insurance policies, and changes in the “ship to” address on my own orders. 2. Create a new spreadsheet called “My address history” with one row per address, newest first: full street address, city, state, ZIP, earliest month I lived there, last month I lived there, how confident you are (confirmed by a lease/closing/USPS email, or inferred from orders/bills), and links to the 2–3 emails that prove each date. 3. Flag any gap or overlap of more than one month between addresses, and list what kind of email would settle it. Only use addresses and dates you can link to an email. If you can’t pin a date down, write “unknown” rather than guess. Don’t include anyone else’s address (gifts, people I shipped to). Don’t fill in or submit any form, sign in anywhere, or contact anyone. I tested this prompt with my own Gmail account, which has messages stretching back more than 20 years. Within a few minutes, Spark spat out a spreadsheet that looked reasonably accurate, piecing together my rental history stretching back to 2006 using everything from lease agreements and move-in notices to security deposit returns and utility confirmations. The spreadsheet also specified which dates Spark was confident about and which ones it wasn’t. For example, it inferred the last month I lived at my oldest address based on various orders and bills that it found. That’s not iron-clad proof that I moved out in a given month, but it’s a solid guess—and more importantly, I know it’s a guess, not fact. This agentic AI prompt could work with a number of other agents, too, including a ChatGPT “dot” agent, Claude Cowork, and Meta Muse (and, in fact, this prompt was inspired by this article about Muse). I tested the prompt with ChatGPT, Claude, and Muse agents and got similar results from all of them, but Spark’s spreadsheet was the most thorough.

item.title: Daft Punk is getting an official Lego set
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Daft Punk is getting an official Lego set A fan-built model of the Alive tour pyramid got the green light to become a real product. Daft Punk is getting the Lego treatment — officially, this time. An upcoming Lego set will pay tribute to the duo's 2007 Alive tour pyramid. The official product is an evolution of a fan-built model that won Lego's Music to Our Ears contest in 2020. Daft Punk and Lego first teased the news on the duo's "WDPK 83.7" YouTube stream, showing a red holographic speaker/Lego brick. A short video accompanying the full announcement shows the duo's minifigures following the same laser brick into a dark landscape, where their console conveniently materializes. Head-bobbing commences, with "Voyager" and "Human After All" making up the soundtrack. The original set was a COVID-era lockdown project by a father and son from Luxembourg. Their glowing pyramid stage includes about 2,000 pieces. A motorized, rotating box of transparent bricks sits inside, recreating the look and feel of the tour's stage spectacle. Lego's designers are working with fan creator Patrick Harboun, who goes by RobotRock, on the final version. This likely won't be the last time the robot DJs show up in Lego. The company's marketing chief, Julia Goldin, described the announcement as "just the beginning of a bigger journey — a creative collab made for fans ready to lose themselves to play." This wasn't even the French duo's first appearance as Lego men: they had a cameo performing "Get Lucky" in the 2024 Lego-animated Pharrell Williams film, Piece By Piece. Lego hasn't yet announced any specific details about the set, including its price or release date. However, it teased that more news will come in 2027.

item.title: Insta360 Mic review: A midrange mic kit that's anything but boring
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Insta360 Mic review: A midrange mic kit that's anything but boring In an ocean of boring microphones, Insta360 adds a (customizable) pop of color. It's been a transformative year for Insta360. The Luna Ultra and Luna Pro cameras, both released over the summer, cemented its reputation as a capable camera-maker that isn't limited to 360 video. When it unveiled the Mic Pro, with its quirky e-ink display, the portfolio of creator products was almost complete. Well, almost, because there was a small gap between the $330 Mic Pro and the affordable Mic Air. Insta360 plugs that gap today with the $250 Mic. Yep, capital M as that's the full name of the product (let's just accept right now this review might get confusing). The Mic is a pared-down version of the Mic Pro, with a cost-saving feature that might actually make it more appealing to many creators. Wireless mic systems are plentiful, but the Insta360 Mic is curious and endearing. The question is, will that be enough to earn it a place on your lapel? I loved the sound on Insta360's Mic Pro and it appears the regular Mic inherited the same audio quality. My voice isn't deep, but it's lower in register and I'm prone to swallowing my words. Recordings with the Mic on default settings and voice mode all sound as clear as a mumbling Brit like me could hope for. Activating the Rich voice tone adds a pleasing amount of presence when speaking, and is, dare I say it, more podcast-friendly. The Bright preset is better for outdoor recording when there's more ambient noise and you want your voice to stand out more, or if you have a particularly low voice, but the standard recording mode remains my preference. Insta360's noise reduction also fares well in both indoor and outdoor environments, without any noticeable artifacting or impact on your voice as can sometimes be the case, especially with cheaper microphones. I prefer to leave any processing to the tools I have on my PC, but the noise cancellation is useful if you're recording in a noisy location and want to share a recording from your phone straight away. I have a few Insta360 cameras — an Ace Pro 2, a Luna Ultra and a Luna Pro — and connecting the Mic directly is easy through on-camera menus. The receiver dongle on the Mic and Mic Pro is pretty chonky and looks conspicuous on a small camera or phone, so being able to ditch it completely is something I really appreciate. One of the more interesting features is the ability to connect four microphones to one receiver. This is great for group interviews or even simple podcasts, especially as you can output each mic to its own audio channel for detailed editing in post. There's also a multi-receiver option, and it's a bit of a hidden gem. I often shoot with two cameras and having my voice record to both at the same time via two receivers saves me some time in editing as I no longer need to worry about keeping a master audio track and syncing the second camera — the audio I want is baked-in to both angles. You can also get creative with this and use a second mic to record ambient sound or another sound source for extra flexibility. On the one hand, the lack of onboard storage is a concession for the lower price. But by introducing removable memory, Insta360 has arguably given the Mic an advantage over the Pro. For starters, you're not limited to the amount of storage built-in to the device, so you can add a large SD card and get many more hours of on-board recording. It also means you can swap out a card should it ever fill up without having to transfer or delete files to make space. Working with additional SD cards is often simpler than connecting the mic via USB to access files. If there are any negatives, it does open up the chance of forgetting your SD card when you need it, and there's the small chance of dust ingress or mechanical failure. But honestly, I feel this is more of a Pro-grade feature in disguise. The e-ink display on the Pro was Insta360's main selling point, and it's just as fun here on the regular Mic. I've heard some people complain about the size of the Mic/Mic Pro transmitters, and they sure are larger than rivals like DJI's Mic 3 or GoPro. However, they are the perfect size for displaying your show's logo, or whatever else you want to upload. It also opens up some creative and even interactive options to drive engagement with your audience if you make videos for YouTube and social media. Take your pick: Rode, DJI, Hollyland and even GoPro. There are multiple options available for creators at various price points. Insta360 is selling the full kit (two transmitters, receiver and case) for $250 which puts it right between Rode's two most popular models: the Wireless Go III and the Wireless Pro. The former is popular, but it's awkward for connecting to phones, while the latter comes with two wired lav mics for a more complete "kit." DJI's most recent mic kits are harder to find in the US, but the popular Mic 3 offers similar functionality to Insta360 with smaller, more discrete transmitters for about the same price. Neither Rode nor DJI have a customizable display, though. Hollyland's Lark 2 kit remains an incredibly popular choice and has similar-sized transmitters, and at $70 it's a staggering value. If you spring for the $300 Lark Max 2, you get wireless monitoring and a slew of other extras. Just remember: The Insta360's Mic and SD card slot remain the main differentiator here. Insta360 knew there was a lot of competition when it launched the Mic Pro. Functionally, it competes well with its rivals, and the e-ink display was a smart addition to make it stand out. With the regular Mic, the Pro's best features remain in a more economical package. The switch from on-board storage to SD card feels smart as it lowers cost while adding genuine practical advantages. But that competition is real. If you just want two microphones and a receiver, better value options are out there. If you own an Insta360 camera, the Mic becomes an easier choice, especially as you can snag just a transmitter for $80. That e-ink display, however, is enough to make the Mic feel genuinely unique in a world of boring, copycat microphones. If you're looking for something that performs well and adds a dash of color or customization to your videos, the Insta360 Mic offers exactly that.

item.title: Roku's Pro Series LX OLED TVs are now available on Amazon
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Roku's Pro Series LX OLED TVs are now available on Amazon It's available as a 55 or 65-inch model. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. The Roku Pro Series LX OLED TVs are now available exclusively on Amazon in 55-inch and 65-inch versions. Roku announced its new OLED TVs in September after years of offering a lineup of more affordable QLED TVs. It started by selling the Pro Series OLED TV models by the time of the announcement at prices that begin at $999. item.title: Momcozy D8 review: I handed my twins’ bottles to a machine, and the daily routine got easier
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
“A pricey, but convenient machine with a trifecta of tricks.”
Quick Recap: Life with twins and a pile of bottles As a mom of twins, I’m always looking for products that make our daily routine a little easier, and the Momcozy D8 has definitely done that. Between constant feedings and what feels like an endless pile of bottles, I need something that’s simple, reliable, and actually saves me time. I love that it holds all the bottles for the day, is easy to use, and drains directly into the sink, so I don’t have to deal with extra cleanup afterward. Bottle care is really three jobs: washing, sterilizing, and drying. Most parents handle them separately, with a sink, a sterilizer, and a drying rack. The D8 does all three in one machine, which is the main reason to consider it over a standalone sterilizer. The Momcozy D8 is a countertop solution that washes, steam-sterilizes, dries, and stores up to eight bottles in one run. In a house with twins, it has become part of the daily routine: I load the day’s bottles, start a cycle, and come back to clean, dry bottles. Each bottle sits over its own spray nozzle, the machine drains through a hose into the sink, and wheels on the base let it move around the counter. It’s not a total nirvana, though. The machine is fairly big. A full wash, sterilize, and dry cycle takes much longer than washing a bottle by hand, and the detergent tablets are a recurring cost. At $359.99, it makes the most sense for families with multiples, exclusive pumpers, and anyone washing a sink full of bottles every day. Parents using one or two bottles a day can get by with less. The D8 is a large appliance, and the size comes from its capacity. There are two racks. The lower one holds up to eight bottles or a full set of breast pump parts, and the upper one is for small pieces like nipples, pacifiers, and straws. The upper rack’s height can be adjusted, so taller items such as a toddler’s water bottle can fit. It accepts wide-neck, narrow, and tall bottles in glass, plastic, or silicone, so you aren’t tied to Momcozy’s own bottles. Setup takes a few minutes. It’s worth reading the manual before the first load, because each rack and holder has a specific place, but loading becomes routine quickly. For all its width, the D8 is short enough to sit under standard upper cabinets, though the lids need some vertical clearance space. It’s worth checking Momcozy’s manual for its water recommendations before the first run. If your tap water is hard, plan to use the descaling cycle regularly to keep mineral buildup in check. One feature I didn’t expect to appreciate as much as I do is the wheels on the bottom, which make it easy to move around the kitchen whenever I need to free up counter space or position it closer to the sink. The wheels sit under removable foot pads, so the machine stays planted until you want to move it. Wherever it lives, the 1.2-meter drain hose has to reach the sink, which in practice keeps the D8 close to it. Momcozy D8 cleaning, sterilizing, and storage What really stood out to me is how thoroughly it cleans. Each bottle gets its own spray nozzle, so I don’t have to worry about whether everything is getting washed properly. Momcozy rates the machine at 64 jets in total. The upper rack uses smaller, more precise jets aimed at nipples, straws, and pacifiers, which are the parts where milk residue tends to collect. Pump parts get rotating spray heads, four of which come in the box, that turn the water through different angles to reach the curved insides of flanges. A separate attachment cleans 5mm pump tubing. The dedicated pump rack is also useful for wearable pumps, which break down into a lot of small pieces that are tedious to scrub by hand. Setting a wearable pump’s milk-collection cup directly over one of the rotating jets pushes water into the narrow channels and valves that a brush struggles to reach. Milk fat leaves a film on plastic that a standard dishwasher doesn’t always clear, and a dedicated bottle washer is designed to handle exactly that. I also appreciate that it does more than just wash. Iit sterilizes, dries, and stores the bottles until I’m ready to use them. After washing, the D8 steam-sterilizes and then dries the load. A full wash, sterilize and dry cycle is long, but none of it is hands-on time, so it’s easy to start after a feeding and get on with the day. Clean items can stay inside for up to 72 hours with the lid closed, while the machine manages moisture so nothing turns musty. That works well for overnight feeds. The modes include Rapid Wash, which Momcozy says takes as little as 19 minutes, plus Normal Wash, Steam Sterilize, Dry, and Storage. Drying deserves a note. Nipples and the bottoms of bottles are the spots most likely to hold water after a full cycle. If anything comes out damp, the standalone Dry mode finishes the job. It’s worth checking before you leave a load in storage. There’s also a self-cleaning mode that descales the internal chamber and pipes and runs a high-temperature pass. Running it regularly keeps milk residue and mineral buildup from accumulating inside the machine. Another nice bonus is that the machine comes with cleaning tablets, so you can start using it right out of the box without having to purchase anything extra. It’s a small detail, but one that makes getting started even more convenient for busy parents. The box includes 60 detergent tablets and four descaling tablets, along with four nipple holders, four pump-part spray assemblies, and the drain hose. The Momcozy D8 has quickly become one of the most-used baby products in our home. Instead of spending time scrubbing bottles after every feeding, I can let it handle the work while I focus on my twins. As a busy mom, I really value products that make everyday tasks more manageable, and this has definitely helped simplify our feeding routine. It’s one of those appliances that earns its spot on the counter because it gets used every single day. That said, it isn’t without its downsides. The unit does have a fairly large footprint, so families with limited counter space may need to rearrange their kitchen to accommodate it. The wash cycles are also longer than quickly cleaning a bottle by hand, so I found it’s most efficient when running a full load instead of just one or two bottles. You’ll also need to restock the cleaning tablets once the included supply runs out. Price is the other consideration. At $359.99, the D8 costs far more than a steam sterilizer with a dryer, which handles everything except the washing. The premium only pays off if you’d actually use the washing and the capacity. While those are things to consider, the overall convenience of having clean, sterilized, dry bottles ready to go has been well worth it for our family, especially with two babies to keep fed. The big conundrum: Washer or sterilizer? Before spending $359.99, it’s worth asking whether you need a washer at all. Most baby bottles are dishwasher-safe, and a dishwasher handles routine cleaning. Sterilizing is the bigger question. The CDC says daily sanitizing is especially important for babies younger than 2 months, babies born prematurely, and those with weakened immune systems. For older, healthy babies, careful cleaning after each use is generally enough. That’s the divide between the two product types. A sterilizer-dryer, which costs considerably less, holds a small amount of water, steams bottles you’ve already washed, and then dries them. A washer, such as the D8, works more like a small countertop dishwasher. It draws from a larger reservoir, uses detergent tablets, sprays the load, sterilizes it with steam, dries it with hot air, and drains through a hose. If you go through a handful of bottles a day, a sterilizer and your existing dishwasher will cover the essentials. The D8 makes sense when the volume is high enough that washing itself becomes the bottleneck. With twins, that’s exactly where we are. Should you buy it? Yes, if you have twins or multiples, exclusively pump, prep bottles for daycare, or wash six to eight bottles and pump parts a day. At that volume, one full cycle replaces several trips to the sink, and the D8’s capacity matches the workload. No, if you use only one or two bottles a day, have very little counter space, or are working with a tight budget. A smaller washer, or a sterilizer-dryer paired with hand-washing, will cover your needs for less. Momcozy KleanPal Pro — The D8 is an upgraded take on this smaller washer, which holds up to four bottles, uses 26 spray jets, offers a 19-minute Rapid Wash, and dries through an H13 HEPA filter. It takes up less counter space and suits families with one baby. Baby Brezza Bottle Washer Pro — This one also washes, sterilizes, and dries in a single countertop unit. You might want to compare its capacity and footprint against the D8, especially if you already use other Baby Brezza products. FAQs (Frequently Asked Questions) How many bottles can you wash at once? It can handle 8 bottles or a full pump kit. Does it have a water tank? No, you don’t have to worry about cleaning a water tank. It features an automatic drain with a built-in hose. Can it handle tiny and hard-to-clean pump parts? Yes, the proprietary Pump360 rotary jets do a reliable clean-up job. Can it handle dried-on milk residues? Yes, the spraying pressure is strong enough, and paired with hot water, it can clean milk fats and other residues.

item.title: Tangerine for Mac makes file conversions seamless with a simple drag-and-drop gesture
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
File conversion on Mac usually involves a frustrating routine of opening dedicated apps or relying on slow web tools that come with privacy risks. A new macOS utility called Tangerine aims to fix this completely. Launched recently by an independent developer, the app reimagines file management by giving you access to a powerful suite of conversion and editing tools with a simple drag and drop. A simplified workflow for quick file conversions Tangerine bypasses traditional user interfaces entirely. Instead of opening a separate window to upload and convert a document, you simply click and drag a file while holding the Shift key. This action summons a sleek radial menu around the cursor displaying all available formatting options for that specific file type. In addition to basic format swaps, the tool wheel provides instant access to advanced features like video and image redaction, audio bleeping, and media compression. You can also trim videos, annotate images, remove metadata, and split or merge PDFs directly from your desktop or any Finder window. Once you make a selection, Tangerine automatically drops the converted file into the exact same folder as the original. Additional shortcuts like dragging with the Command or Control keys reveal extra wheels for specific tools and quick actions like AirDrop. The app supports 275 conversion options and 26 file tools, along with 6 file actions. That friction-free file conversion comes at a premium, though. Tangerine will set you back $29.99, but there’s a free trial available to let you test it out before committing. The free trial gives you 20 conversions to start, after which the app locks you down to just the action wheel. The app supports all Apple silicon Macs running macOS 13 or later. If $30 is a bit too steep for a utility app, there’s a compelling, completely free alternative worth checking out. OpenShelf is an open-source menu bar app that uses a similar drag-and-drop action wheel to let you quickly convert, edit, or stash files on temporary floating shelves. It’s available for free, making it an easy pick for anyone who loves Tangerine’s feature set but can’t justify its premium price tag.

item.title: This GEEKOM mini PC makes me wonder why people even buy desktops
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
I've been building PCs for over 20 years, so naturally, I get why people do it: it's fun, and you get a great computer at the end. But beyond the fun, is there any reason to spend the time and money anymore when a plug-and-play mini PC can absolutely replace your daily driver for almost anything but gaming? - Intel Core Ultra 7 356H (16 cores, 16 threads, up to 4.7GHz) - Intel Graphics (integrated, 4 Xe3 cores) GEEKOM's latest mini PC packs a lot of power in a small footprint. It has a highly capable CPU and NPU combo and it can easily replace most people's daily driver. - 32GB DDR5-5600 (SO-DIMM, upgradeable to 64GB) - 1TB (upgradeable) - Powerful performance in a tiny package - Great connectivity, including 2.5G Ethernet and Wi-Fi 7 The GEEKOM IT13 2026 mini PC is available directly from GEEKOM and Amazon. Both sell it for $1,399, which is a discount from its MSRP of $1,689. - 2x USB4 (40Gbps), 4x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 (10Gbps), 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x SD 4.0 card reader, 1x 2.5GbE Ethernet, 1x 3.5mm combo jack, DC in - 4.61 x 4.41 x 1.94 inches (117 x 112 x 49.2mm) - 1.29 pounds (586g) - Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, 2.5GbE Ethernet - Intel AI Boost (50 TOPS) - 120W DC adapter (19V/6.32A); 100W USB-C PD input supported GEEKOM's IT13 is a tiny box of many possibilities As I use a massive desktop tower as my daily driver, I think I may have underestimated GEEKOM's latest take on a mini PC. Testing it quickly cleared that up for me, though. This mini PC, while truly tiny (1.29 pounds), is a beast in more ways than one. It weighs less than my laptop, all the while offering performance far above what many laptops can provide. I'll dig into the numbers in a second, but let's start with a big-picture overview of what we're dealing with. The IT13 has excellent build quality. The metal frame definitely adds a bit of weight, but it's negligible given its small footprint. It feels and looks premium, though, with a nice blue-ish finish that sets it apart from similar PCs. As far as ports go, you have a full-fledged desktop on your hands, with more connectivity than many ATX motherboards can provide. Two USB4 (40Gbps) ports, four USB-A 3.2 Gen 2, two HDMI, one 2.5GbE Ethernet, an audio jack, and an SD card reader is plenty enough for my needs, although I would've liked a front-facing USB4 port. I know it's a small thing to many, but other than the lack of a front-facing USB4/USB-C, I like the way the manufacturer planned the ports here. You can plug in up to four screens, so those cables would be a pain to deal with if they weren't exactly where they are: at the back of the PC. Taking it apart was easy, and as it's upgradeable, that's noteworthy. I like that the screws are attached. You can add up extra RAM, although the 32GB DDR5 that it comes with should be plenty for what most people are going to use it for. You can also add extra storage up to 4TB. Despite the tiny form factor, temperatures don't appear to be a problem for this mini PC. It averages 51 to 58 degrees Celsius during my benchmarks, although running 3DMark Steel Nomad Light (GPU test) made the CPU spike up to 74 degrees. No biggie, though. The box remained quiet throughout every test. It got warm to the touch at times, and the back vents did a good job of expelling hot air. I've certainly had laptops that performed worse while heating up more, so in this regard, it's a full 10/10 for GEEKOM's IT13. I put this mini PC through its paces, and it kept up throughout Under the hood, the IT13 runs on Intel's Core Ultra 7 356H, part of the Core Ultra Series 3 family, which you probably know as Panther Lake. It packs 16 cores without Hyper-Threading, with four Cougar Cove P-cores, eight Darkmont E-cores, and four low-power E-cores. As we all know, raw benchmark numbers mean very little when viewed in a vacuum. To make sense of these scores, I compared this model to the other mini PCs we've recently reviewed here at How-To Geek, including the Acemagic K5 and the Lenovo Yoga Mini Gen 11. GEEKOM's own IT13 Max is another interesting point of comparison. In Geekbench 7, the IT13 2026 scored 2,430 in single-core and 15,504 in multi-core, which actually puts it ahead of the IT13 Max by roughly 14% and 8%, respectively. The Yoga Mini leads the charge by about 4% and 10%. Geekbench 6 showed similar results, although the multi-core score turned out to be much closer when we compare the two GEEKOM PCs. Cinebench 2026 backed that up, with the IT13 landing about 11% and 17% ahead of the IT13 Max. The Yoga Mini maintains a lead, but it's a subtle win that won't be felt in real-world performance. 7-Zip benchmarks flipped the situation around a little bit. The older GEEKOM pulled ahead thanks to the extra threads on the Core Ultra 9 185H. However, the results are all close enough for these PCs that we're not talking about a make-it-or-break-it type of situation. GEEKOM's IT13 has a powerhouse of an NPU, and it shows up in benchmarks The AI capabilities are definitely there The 50 TOPS that the Core Ultra 7 356H is rated at is enough to clear Microsoft's 40 TOPS bar for Copilot+ PC features with room to spare. It also sets the IT13 apart from other, more budget-oriented mini PCs, like the Acemagic K5—which, while equipped with an NPU, is nowhere near as capable. The scores speak for themselves. I tested the CPU and the NPU using Geekbench AI, and through Intel's OpenVINO framework, the NPU scored 34,822 in half-precision and 54,006 in quantized, which is about 21x and 7x faster than the CPU. The Acemagic K5 was left in the dust. These scores bode well for this PC's capabilities when it comes to running local AI. item.title: Carbonite Professional Review: Peace-of-Mind Backup That Needs More Features
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Carbonite is an automated, business-focused cloud backup service designed to keep your data safe through encryption protocols supporting HIPAA, FRPA, and GLBA compliance. Its simple plans and easy-to-navigate apps make it a worthwhile choice for small business owners who want to create backups with minimal fuss. Since our last review, Carbonite has also improved its security options. However, Carbonite doesn't include as much data storage as rival services, including Editors' Choice winner Acronis Cyber Protect. In addition, its limited mobile apps don't let you backup files created on your phone. Carbonite offers three Professional plans for consultants, freelancers, and other small business owners (each covers 25 computers). The most affordable plan, Core, costs $24 per month ($287.99 annually) and includes 250GB of automated, encrypted cloud backups. The mid-tier plan, Power, is $66.58 per month ($799 annually) and ups the cloud storage to 500GB. The top-tier plan, Ultimate, costs $108.25 per month ($1,299.99 annually) and connects to unlimited servers. Like Power, the plan includes 500GB of cloud backups. Want more than the relatively skimpy 500GB of storage? You must pay an additional $100 per year for every 100GB added to your plan. You'll almost certainly pay those fees using Carbonite across 25 PCs. By contrast, Acronis Cyber Protect has unlimited storage for Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 shops. iDrive's 25-device Business tier includes 1.25 TB of storage and costs just $349.99 for the first year (and $499.50 annually thereafter). You'd spend more than $1,000 per year to get an equivalent amount of cloud storage from the Carbonite Backup Ultimate plan. Carbonite's parent company, OpenText, also offers specialized security services, including OpenText Core Endpoint Backup for businesses with 26 or more devices and/or large numbers of employees. The services have custom pricing plans, so you must book a consultation for a quote. Installing Carbonite is simple and fast. You can leverage or modify the default settings in the Advanced Settings area to suit your needs. We went with the default settings (continuously backing up my files), but you can prompt Carbonite to only back up files once per day or avoid creating backups during specific hours. This is similar to the range of scheduling options with Acronis Cyber Protect and other top-ranking backup apps. Carbonite backed up our computer within a couple of minutes. You add team member details after booting up Carbonite. You can manually enter the information, copy and paste it into fields, or import it from a spreadsheet. You can also set each team member's permission level to either User or Administrator. Each person receives a link with instructions for setting up Carbonite on their devices, so you don't have to worry about walking them through the process. The Groups feature lets you organize employees by department, policy type, or other criteria. This simplifies finding specific users and viewing how much storage each department uses. You can then click on any user's name to manage their policies, assign additional devices to them, and perform remote data restoration. You can use Carbonite's valet installation service (included with the subscription) if you're less technically inclined or too busy to figure it out yourself. With it, a Carbonite representative installs the software and walks you through the relevant settings. Your entire organization can use this service, helping your business get quickly backed up without eating into your work time. Policies dictate what is backed up on each device connected to your Carbonite account. The Carbonite Default policy—which your computers will automatically be set to—backs up the Desktop, Documents, Outlook Data, Pictures, Music, and Videos folders. You can't alter this policy, but you can add new policies to customize the data backed up on a specific device. The process is simple: You can choose specific folders, add folders not included in the main list, and exclude file types. This gives you full control over the data Carbonite keeps from every computer and server connected to your account. Carbonite has three main options: Settings & Controls, Get My Files Back, and View My Backup. Settings & Controls is where you change how often Carbonite backs up your files. You can also toggle colored dots to signal the backup status of your files and folders. Files with full, up-to-date backups are marked with a green dot, while files with in-progress or scheduled backups are marked with orange dots. Partial green dots indicate that a folder contains parts without backups enabled (but everything with backups enabled is up to date). You can also use this area to enable hard drive scanning (so Carbonite can find files to back up), reduce Carbonite's internet usage, pause backups, or instantly create backups for anything in the queue. Get My Files Back gives you two options: restore all your data or restore specific files and folders. If you restore all data, Carbonite automatically maps files to their original locations (unless you ask it not to). If you restore specific files and folders, you're sent to the Carbonite website to choose what to resurrect. You can quickly move between major folders (like documents and pictures) via the sidebar, search for a specific folder or file using the search bar, or scroll the dropdown menu to see what's available. Carbonite stores up to 12 versions of your files, including daily versions for every day of the past week, weekly versions for the past three weeks, and monthly versions for the past two months. With just a few clicks, you can restore these version files from the Carbonite Backup Drive on your computer or the Carbonite website. The process is pretty smooth. Carbonite's Android and iOS mobile apps make it easy to view your backups and pull files from computers connected to your account onto your phone. They're helpful, but navigating the folders on a small screen is a bit cumbersome. You can make things simpler by marking your most important files as Favorites. These marked files are moved to a separate area where you can quickly access them without combing through all your folders. This makes it easy to grab the latest backups of your most important documents. Unfortunately, the Carbonite mobile app can't create file backups on your mobile device. If you simply want to sync files from your phone to your backup drive, consider Google Drive or Microsoft OneDrive. Carbonite uses Transport Layer Security to protect all files in transit during the backup process and Blowfish 128-bit encryption to keep your data safe once in the cloud. You can also enable private encryption keys, AES 256-bit encryption codes generated from a passphrase. You must enter the passphrase or the encryption key to access backups. Carbonite also protects your data using the proprietary Carbonite File System. Although the Carbonite site doesn’t disclose exactly how this works, it states that it complies with HIPAA, FERPA, and GLBA standards. These security measures are great, but not as extensive as the tools in other backup software. For example, you can't password-lock individual files like Microsoft OneDrive for Business. However, at least you can now set up two-factor authentication, a major security upgrade Carbonite previously lacked. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. However, the storage limits—and the steep cost of adding more—make Carbonite less appealing than competitors such as Acronis Cyber Protect (our Editors' Choice winner for business cloud backup) and iDrive. Likewise, the inability to backup your Android and iOS devices is disappointing, considering that business-centric Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive cloud storage apps let you do so with ease. item.title: Best PCIe 4.0 SSDs 2026: 5 top picks from the PC experts
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Recent computing equipment typically supports the 16Gbps PCIe 4.0 protocol as its baseline data transfer/SSD storage technology. While Gen 4 is slowly being supplanted by 32Gbps PCIe 5.0 (most computers mix the two), the difference in real-world performance is not as great as you might think. A lot of software, which unfortunately includes Windows, can’t take full advantage. Alas, PCIe 5.0 still demands a hefty surcharge. As to surcharges… At the time we were bringing this article up to date, SSD prices were soaring and availability shrinking — thanks in large part to the AI gold rush. Hence, the newly researched prices shown below will not match the older ones in the linked reviews. The recommendations below represent the cream of the nearly three dozen PCIe 4.0 SSDs that we’ve reviewed, best suited for a variety of needs. Whether you want to upgrade or add more storage, there’s a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD for you. Read on to learn more, including what to look for. Why you should trust PCWorld for PCIe 4.0 SSD reviews and buying advice: We’re not called PCWorld for nothing. Our reviewers have been testing PC hardware for decades. Our storage evaluations are exhaustive, testing the limits of every product — from performance benchmarks to the practicalities of regular use. As PC users ourselves, we know what makes a killer product stand out. Only the best SSDs have made our list of picks. WD Black SN7100 SSD/SanDisk Optimux GX 7100 – Best PCIe 4.0 SSD - Slower random performance than DRAM designs Who should buy the WD Black SN7100/Optimus GX 7100? Those looking for top sequential performance for a bit less money should be all over the WD Black SN7100, which is still available under that name but will be sold as the SanDisk Optimux GX 7100 going forward. (SanDisk was acquired, then recently divested by WD.) We were wowed by the 2TB SN7100’s host memory buffer (HMB) performance, though it was supplanted as number one by an extremely narrow margin by the Lexar Play 2280. However, unlike the latter, we were still able to find the Black SN7100 for sale online at the time of this writing, hence it’s our best of pick. WD Black SN7100/SanDisk Optimus GX 7100: Further considerations There’s a trade-off with HMB (host memory buffer) design SSDs, such as the SN7100. They use the host system’s memory for primary caching duties, which can actually result in slightly faster sequential transfers, but weaker random performance. In other words, DRAM drives offer significantly better random/4K file performance if that’s what you’re looking for. Why might you want better random performance? For a slightly snappier OS experience, though this can be very hard to spot with the naked eye. The Black SN7100 carries the industry standard five-year warranty / 600TBW rating (terabytes that can be written) per TB, and you’re looking at probably the best PCIe 4.0 SSD for average users as well as gamers. WD SN5100/SanDisk Optimus 5100 – Best budget PCIe 4.0 SSD - Very good PCIe 4.0 performer for most workloads - Single-sided design fits in just about any 2280 slot - QLC slows down during very long writes Who should buy the WD Blue SN5100/SanDisk Optimus 5100? It’s hard to describe any SSD these days as “budget,” but you will currently save quite a few bucks with this DRAM-less (HMB/Host Memory Buffer) design. Once available at 2TB for $150, that drive is now $285. Thanks, OpenAI. That said, the SN5100, now remonikered as the SanDisk Optimus 5100, is still available which can’t be said for a lot of the competition. The WD Blue SN5100 is the successor to our former bargain pick — the WD Blue SN5000. The newer drive does better in most tests, most markedly in sustained/sequential throughput. At the moment, the pricing is exactly the same, so we say go with the faster of the two. WD Blue SN5100/SanDisk Optimus 5100: Further considerations In our testing, the Blue SN5100 ranked third among all the HMB SSDs we’ve tested — and was first by a large margin writing our 450GB file. You lose nothing in sequential performance these days with HMB. The drive sports a five-year warranty limited by a TBW rating (terabytes that may be written) of 600TBW per 1TB of capacity. SanDisk Optimus GX 7100M NVMe SSD – Best PCIe 4.0 SSD for Steam Deck - The fastest PCIe 4.0 SSD I’ve tested to date - 2230 form factor fits handheld gaming devices Who should buy the Sandisk Optimus GX 7100M? For gaming handheld owners, the Optimus GX 7100M is a win-win. Naturally, it’s the correct 2230 form factor that handhelds such as the Steam Deck require. But the GX 7100M stomps the short-body competition with exceptional performance. We’re talking the fastest 2230 SSD we’ve tested — nay, the fastest PCIe 4.0 SSD of any size we’ve tested. The fact that it’s particularly dominant in 4K performance is noteworthy given that the GX 7100M is an HMB (host memory buffer) design, which historically has been relatively weak with 4K. Sandisk Optimus GX 7100M: Further considerations Okay, yeah, this SSD is pretty pricey. For instance, it’s currently about $20 more than the 1TB version of the Crucial P310 — our previous pick for the Steam Deck — and over $100 more than the 2TB version of the Crucial P310. That’s a steep premium. That being said, if you want the absolute fastest 2230 SSD for your gaming handheld, the GX 7100M is it. If you can find it for less than MSRP — which seems likely to happen over time — all the better! Seagate Game Drive – Best PCIe 4.0 SSD for PS5 - Twice the TBW rating of the competition Who should buy the Seagate Game Drive PS5 NVMe SSD? The Seagate Game Drive PS5 NVMe SSD is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD aimed specifically at next-gen game consoles — the PS5 in particular. It doesn’t disappoint, using DRAM for primary caching duties, which is almost essential to wring top performance out of Sony’s console system. The PS5 doesn’t support HMB, so without DRAM SSD you’re relying exclusively on an HMB SSD’s slower secondary caching. The Game Drive ships in 1TB and 2TB capacities, so you’ll have plenty of space to store all of your games. Note that when I checked recently (March 2026), this drive was still available, but in short supply. Seagate Game Drive PS5 NVMe SSD: Further considerations While the Seagate Game Drive is optimized for a PS5, it’s perfectly viable with any computing device with a PCIe M.2 2280 slot. It did remarkably well in our performance testing, earning the spot as the second-fastest PCIe 4.0 SSD to date with random ops. Seagate provides a generous five-year warranty with the drive and it has an astounding 1,275TBW rating — more than double the industry norm. PS5 owners simply can’t go wrong with the Seagate Game Drive. Corsair MP600 Micro – Best 2242 form-factor SSD Who should buy the Corsair MP600 Micro? The Corsair MP600 Micro fills a niche for devices that can accommodate an SSD that’s larger than the 2230 form factor used by handheld gaming consoles, but can’t accept a standard 2280 modules that are used in most PCs and laptops. We’re talking about the 2242 form factor — meaning 22mm wide by 42mm long. Corsair MP600 Micro: Further considerations Lenovo started the 2242 trend with its Legion Go and Thinkpad portables and there are now respectable storage upgrade options — the best of which is the Corsair MP600 Micro. The MP600 Micro isn’t the fastest PCIe 4.0 SSD we’ve tested, but it was the fastest 2242 type and turned in a performance that compared well against many 2280 SSDs. - Samsung 990: Slower than the older 990 EVO Plus and not a bargain, even given the current NAND crunch. - Orico OS5: This drive is marketed for the PS5, but uses a non-supported HMB design. - Teamgroup T-Create C47: Stands out in super-long writes. - Lexar NQ780: Makes a very good showing in a field of stiff competition. - Orico IG740-Pro: Fast enough, decently affordable SSD that ships with some nice-to-have extras. - PNY CS2342: A 2230 small form-factor SSD sized for Steam Deck, which performs very well with light workloads. - Teamgroup MP44Q: A great everyday performer. - Addlink A93/S93: A solid-performing PCIe 4.0, DRAM-less NVMe SSD that might save you a few bucks. But the A93 with its heatsink faces heavy competition from many similarly priced and often faster SSDs. - WD SN850X 8TB SSD: Far faster than the previously tested 2TB version, but currently you’ll pay a staggering premium for it. - 990 EVO Plus: An update to Samsung’s 990 EVO hybrid drive that can use either the PCIe 4.0 or PCIe 5.0 interface — although the latter is limited to PCIe 4.0’s theoretical bandwidth. - T-Force G50: This drive should be on your short list. It’s a relatively inexpensive, solid performing PCIe 4.0 drive for everyday tasks. - Kingston NV3: Proof that DRAM-less drives — those that use a Host Memory Buffer (HMB) as cache — can offer competitive performance. - Sabrent Rocket Nano 2242: Features a smaller form factor (22mm x 42mm) that was tailor-made for Lenovo’s Legion Go and Thinkpads — but can also be used in a standard slot as well. Drive tests for most of the drives listed above utilized Windows 11, 64-bit running on an X790 (PCIe 4.0/5.0) motherboard/i5-12400 CPU combo with two Kingston Fury 32GB DDR5 4800MHz modules (64GB of memory total). Both 20Gbps USB and Thunderbolt 4 are integrated to the back panel and Intel CPU/GPU graphics are used. The 48GB transfer tests utilize an ImDisk RAM disk taking up 58GB of the 64GB of total memory. The 450GB file is transferred from a 2TB Samsung 990 Pro which also runs the OS. Newer SSDs were tested with Windows 11 24H2, 64-bit running off of a PCIe 4.0 Samsung 990 Pro in an Asus Z890-Creator WiFi (PCIe 4.0/5.0) motherboard. The CPU is a Core Ultra i5 225 feeding/fed by two Crucial 64GB DDR5 5600MHz modules (128GB of memory total). Both 20Gbps USB and Thunderbolt 5 are integrated and Intel CPU/GPU graphics are used. SSDs involved in the test are mounted in either a HighPoint 7604A 16x 4-slot PCIe 5.0 RAID adapter card or a single-slot Asus ROG M.2 PCIe 5.0 adapter. We run the CrystalDiskMark 8, AS SSD 2, and ATTO 4 synthetic benchmarks to find the storage device’s potential performance, then a series of 48GB and 450GB transfers tests using Windows Explorer drag-and-drop to show what you’ll see under Window, as well as the far faster FastCopy to show what’s possible. A two-drive 25GBps RAID 0 array on the HighPoint 7604A 16x PCIe 5.0 adapter card is used as the secondary source/destination. Each test is performed on a newly formatted and TRIM’d drive so the results are optimal. Note that in normal use, as a drive fills up, performance may decrease due to less NAND for secondary caching, as well as other factors. This can be less of a factor with the current crop of SSDs with far faster late-generation NAND. Caveat: The performance numbers shown apply only to the drive we were shipped and to the capacity tested. SSD performance can and will vary by capacity due to more or fewer chips to shotgun reads/writes across and the amount of NAND available for secondary caching. Vendors also occasionally swap components. If you ever notice a large discrepancy between the performance you experience and that which we report, by all means, let us know. To learn more about our testing methodology see PCWorld’s article on how we test internal SSDs. Jon L. Jacobi was around when computing meant flipping switches, and has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state drives. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for more than two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. There are a few things to look out for when purchasing a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, but most importantly you’ll want to focus on capacity, price, and warranty length. Three-year warranties are standard with bargain drives, but nicer models are generally guaranteed for up to five years. A good indicator of expected longevity is an SSD’s TBW (terabytes written) rating which mitigates the warranty period like the miles in an automobile warranty. This is the number of terabytes the vendor thinks you’ll be able to write before it runs out of extra (overprovisioned) cells to replace worn ones. This is an equation based on the type of NAND being used, but also incorporates financial concerns. I.e., the cost of replacing the drive should it not last as long the rating. Unlike the early days of SSDs and NAND, modern drives won’t generally wear out with normal consumer usage, as Tech Report tested and proved years ago with a grueling endurance test. We’re talking petabytes of writes in many cases. That said, QLC NAND generally carries a lower TBW rating than TLC NAND. Another crucial thing to watch out for is the technology used to connect the SSD to your PC. For more details and buying advice see below, or you can read our in-depth guide on which type of SSD you should buy. PCIe: This is the standard modern memory transfer bus, to the tune of nearly 4GBps over PCIe gen 3 and well over 10GBps when you reach PCIe 5.0. The transport technology pairs nicely with the NVMe protocol (see the next entry) used by all modern M.2 PCIe SSDs. Most M.2 slots (some older ones are SATA — see below) are PCIe and you can buy adapters that allow you to employ “gumstick” (2280) M.2 drives in a PCIe slot. PCIe 4.0 drives are significantly faster than PCIe 3.0, but require an AMD Ryzen 3000-series or Intel Core 11th-gen (or newer) processor, along with a compatible PCIe 4.0 motherboard. PCIe 5.0 is even faster — up to 15GBps with storage. NVMe: Non-Volatile Memory Express technology takes advantage of PCIe’s bountiful bandwidth and the unique properties of NAND such as multiple lanes and caching to create blisteringly fast SSD performance. Check out PCWorld’s “Everything you need to know about NVMe” for a nitty-gritty deep-dive. M.2: You might assume all M.2 drives are PCIe/NVMe. However, before NVMe was a thing, some M.2 slots and SSDs were mSATA. If you’re shopping to upgrade an older computer make sure which technology you need — NVMe or SATA. mSATA and U.2: You may also stumble across mSATA in older equipment, and U.2 SSDs for enterprise-grade servers and the like, but consumer motherboard support is almost nil for the latter. Speed matters, of course, but most modern SSDs, even the slower ones are ridiculously fast — so don’t overbuy. A PCIe SSD will only perform as fast as the generation of the device it’s installed in. In other words, don’t expect a PCIe 5.0 SSD to perform at its rated speed on a PCIe 3.0 computer. Speaking of which, you can expect roughly 3.5GBps max from PCIe 3.0, 7.5GBps max from PCIe 4.0, and somewhere just north of 14GBps with PCIe 5.0 under optimal conditions — i.e., using synthetic benchmarks or software that supports NVMe’s multiple queues. Single-queue Windows limits all flavors to under 4GBps during normal transfers, so again — don’t overbuy in terms of performance. Note: If you want better transfer performance from your SSDs, check out FastCopy. It can transfer files two to three times faster than Windows Explorer. What is the best PCIe 4.0 SSD? PCWorld’s top pick for a PCIe 4.0 SSD is the WD Black SN7100 in up to 4TB of capacity. The 2TB version that we tested was the second-fastest PCIe 4.0 SSD overall in our benchmarks, but is still available, while the ever-so-slightly faster Lexar Play 2280 doesn’t seem to be. What is the best cheap PCIe 4.0 SSD? The best cheap SSD in our view is the WD Blue SN5100, followed closely by Kingston’s NV3. Both of these PCIe 4.0 SSDs are fast and relatively affordable. What is the best PCIe 4.0 SSD for a gaming console? Essentially, gaming consoles are computers so the same SSDs that are best for PCs are the also best for gaming consoles. That said, the excellent performance and super-generous TBW rating of Seagate’s Game Drive PS5 NVMe SSD makes it our current choice. The DRAM design (which uses onboard memory for secondary caching) results in class-leading random ops performance, as well a full compatibility with PS5. What is the best brand for a PCIe 4.0 SSD? If you want the best guarantees look to Seagate, some of their pricier models have two to three times the TBW rating and a period of free data recovery is also provided. Samsung and WD are also long-standing favorites with well-earned reputations for quality products. That said, nearly all vendors use the same controllers and NAND as the big boys. The differences generally lie in support and warranty periods. In other words, there aren’t any real dogs among relatively well-known SSD sellers. Are SSDs good for long-term storage? SSDs are excellent for long-term storage, though that depends on what you consider long term. Theoretically, the NAND memory cells, which are voltage traps, could leak over time and become unreadable, but in the decade or so that SSDs have been in heavy use, we’ve not seen this type of degradation. Short answer, a couple of decades, yes; a couple of millennia, perhaps not.
