item.title: Obsbot Meet Flip review: This tiny 4K webcam folds away for privacy and portability
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
The Obsbot Meet Flip is an impressive travel camera for laptops and the workplace. The foldable housing protects the lens, while the integrated stand eliminates the need for a separate monitor mount. The 4K image is rich in detail in good lighting, and the autofocus is fast. It’s a shame that Windows Hello is missing and that a carrying case isn’t included. This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Many laptop cameras still produce a flat image and quickly lose detail in moderate room lighting. The Obsbot Meet Flip aims to solve this problem without taking up much space in your bag. We tested the $119 4K webcam on Windows 11 using Microsoft Teams and Obsbot Center. We used firmware version 4.5.4.1 and Center version 2.0.15.186. The name aptly describes the core feature of the Meet Flip. The camera module is mounted on a wide hinge and can be folded completely into the stand. The lens then faces inwards and is mechanically covered. At the same time, the camera switches to standby mode. A status LED indicates when the camera is active. This means privacy is protected with a single hand movement. A separate lens cover or a purely electronic shut-off is not necessary. When folded, the webcam measures 1.63 × 1.76 × 0.74 inches. When open, the dimensions are 1.63 × 1.45 × 1.25 inches. Weighing just 1.34 ounces, it’s barely noticeable in a laptop bag. The difference is particularly striking when compared to the Logitech Brio 4K: At 4 inches, its camera housing is more than twice as wide. The Meet Flip therefore takes up very little space, even on narrow laptop lids. The test unit is well-built. The plastic casing feels sturdy, and the hinge reliably holds the selected angle. Rubberized contact surfaces protect the screen and ensure a secure grip on flat monitor casings. The manufacturer specifies a maximum screen thickness of 0.80 inches and a recommended tilt range of 0 to 77 degrees. The mount can be opened further mechanically, but it does not fit every thick or heavily curved monitor. The underside features a 1/4-inch thread for attaching to a tripod. The camera can be used in landscape or portrait orientation. Overhead mounting is also possible. The USB-C port is located on the back. The included 4.9-foot cable is relatively stiff and can displace the camera, which weighs just 1.34 ounces, while adjusting its position. A USB-A adapter is also included in the package. A carrying case is missing, even though the Meet Flip is clearly designed for mobile use. The design has a practical limitation. As there is no built-in infrared camera, the Meet Flip does not support Windows Hello login. The larger Logitech Brio 4K remains an attractive option for users who require precisely this feature or a wider field of view. On the other hand, those who frequently switch between the office and working from home will clearly benefit from the Obsbot camera’s smaller footprint. Obsbot offers a remote control for $39.99 and an extendable tripod for $42.49 as accessories. The tripod fits the existing 1/4-inch thread and makes it easier to position the camera away from the monitor. Both extras are optional. Thanks to the standard thread, cheaper tripods from other manufacturers also work. Windows recognizes the Meet Flip as a UVC webcam. In Microsoft Teams, it was immediately available as a camera once plugged in. No driver installation was required. Obsbot Center is used for the advanced features. When launched for the first time, you can choose between a straightforward ‘Lite’ mode and the full ‘Pro’ interface. This makes it easier to get started, as the range of features is impressive for such a small webcam. The software supports 4K at 30 frames per second, as well as 1080p and 720p at either 30 or 60 frames per second. Exposure, white balance, and focus can be adjusted automatically or manually. Brightness, contrast, and saturation can also be adjusted. Sharpness and color cast can also be adjusted. An anti-flicker mode reduces the typical flickering caused by light sources in the 50Hz mains supply. For sleep mode, you can set it to activate automatically and configure a dedicated standby screen. Auto-framing recognizes individuals and small groups. The software can switch between close-up, upper-body, and full-body views. This works in both landscape and portrait orientation. As the Meet Flip does not have a motorized head, tracking is achieved through digital cropping. It responds reliably at a desk, but reaches its limits with fast or wide movements. A hand gesture activates tracking, while another switches to 2x magnification. The software allows for a digital zoom of up to 4x. The virtual camera allows background effects, picture-in-picture views and overlays to be output to Teams or other programmes. A teleprompter and Smart Eye Tracking assist with presentations. Obsbot Center can manage up to four cameras and supports control via Elgato Stream Deck and OSC (Open Sound Control). Obsbot Live connects the webcam directly to a streaming platform. The numerous functions are easily accessible, though the Pro interface does require a bit of getting used to at first. For a standard video conference, the presets in Lite mode are sufficient. AI Magic Notes creates a transcript during a meeting, highlights key passages, and summarizes the main points. Tasks and decisions can also be identified. The feature works with Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and Google Meet, among others. AI Magic Notes includes 120 free minutes. After that, a paid subscription is required. 120 minutes cost $4 per month. The Meet Flip features a stacked 1/2-inch CMOS sensor with 48 megapixels. The f/1.8 lens records 4K at 30 frames per second. In Full HD, 60 frames per second are possible. The phase-detection autofocus captures subjects from around 4 inches away. The diagonal field of view is 72 degrees in 16:9 aspect ratio. In daylight and under normal room lighting, the camera delivers a sharp, well-balanced image. Faces and clothing show more fine detail than with typical laptop cameras. The automatic exposure control keeps bright areas under control, while dark clothing remains clearly defined. HDR helps with windows or lights, but does not completely compensate for extreme differences. The autofocus locks on quickly and without noticeable hunting. This is handy when a product is held briefly in front of the camera. 4K also offers scope for digital cropping. Many video conferencing services stream at Full HD at most. In such cases, the higher sensor resolution primarily improves downscaling and auto-framing. In low light, faces remain clearly recognizable. In dark areas, however, image noise increases and fine textures appear softer. An additional desk lamp visibly improves the result. In daylight, the automatic white balance works reliably. Under warm artificial lighting, the camera tended to produce slightly warm skin tones in our test. In Obsbot Center, the color temperature can be manually adjusted from 2,000 to 10,000 Kelvin. For capturing movement, 1080p at 60 frames per second is often more suitable. Gestures appear smoother, and the lower resolution places less strain on the computer and the connection. 4K30 is suitable for quiet presentations or local recordings. The 4x digital zoom noticeably sacrifices detail. The image remains usable up to the 2x level. The Meet Flip combines an omnidirectional microphone with a directional one. You can choose between a directional mode for individuals, a bidirectional mode for conversations, and Smart Omni for groups. Pure Audio outputs the unprocessed sound on separate channels. In the other modes, automatic gain control and AI noise cancellation are active. Voices are clearly audible at a desk. Depending on the mode, distance, and keyboard used, keystrokes may still be audible. For streams or voice recordings, a separate microphone produces a fuller sound. In terms of price, the Meet Flip sits sensibly between its sister models. The Meet SE costs $69, but is limited to Full HD and uses a smaller sensor. The Meet 2 also delivers 4K, costs $149 euros and, with its separate mount, is less suitable for travel. For mobile users, the Meet Flip offers the best balance between image quality and space requirements. Should you buy the Obsbot Meet Flip? The Obsbot Meet Flip convincingly delivers on its promise of portability. It fits easily into a laptop bag, requires no separate monitor mount and protects the lens when folded away. It’s quick to set up at your desk. The 4K image is impressive in good light, with plenty of detail, and the phase-detection autofocus responds reliably. OBSBOT Centre enhances the camera with auto-framing, gesture control and handy presentation features. At 129 euros, the package is fairly priced. The Meet SE, which is 30 euros cheaper, is sufficient if Full HD is enough. The Meet 2 normally costs $129 and is better suited to a fixed workspace. A Logitech Brio 4K remains an attractive option thanks to Windows Hello and its wider field of view, but it takes up considerably more space. With the Meet Flip, the lack of Windows Hello and the fact that a carrying case isn’t included are the main drawbacks. However, for those who frequently work on the move and are looking for a very compact 4K webcam, it still comes highly recommended. - Sensor: Stacked 1/2-inch CMOS, 48 megapixels - Maximum resolution: 3,840 × 2,160 pixels at 30 frames per second - Additional video modes: 1,920 × 1,080 and 1,280 × 720 pixels at 30 or 60 frames per second - Field of view: 72 degrees diagonally at 16:9, 79.1 degrees at 4:3 - Focus: PDAF autofocus and manual focus, from 10 centimetres to infinity - Image functions: HDR, auto-framing, smart eye tracking, gesture control - Privacy protection: Mechanical lens cover that folds in, automatic sleep mode - Shutter speed: 1/12,800 to 1/30 second - Microphones: One omnidirectional and one directional microphone, AI noise reduction - Microphone modes: Directional, bidirectional, Smart Omni and Pure Audio - Connections: USB-C, USB 2.0, 5 volts/0.4 amps - Mounting: Integrated monitor stand and 1/4-inch thread - Maximum screen thickness: 20.5 millimetres - Recommended tilt range: 0 to 77 degrees - Dimensions when open: 41.6 × 36.9 × 31.9 millimetres - Dimensions when folded: 41.6 × 44.9 × 18.8 millimetres - System requirements: Windows 10 (64-bit) or later, macOS 11 or later - Software: OBSBOT Center and OBSBOT Live, virtual camera, teleprompter, overlays, Stream Deck and OSC control, AI Magic Notes - Contents: Webcam, 1.5-metre USB-C cable, USB-C to USB-A adapter and quick start guide - Optional accessories: Obsbot Meet remote control for $39.99, extendable tripod for $42.49 This article originally appeared on our sister publication PC-WELT and was translated and localized from German.

item.title: Forget eBay. Your local university is a gold mine for cheap PC gear
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
By now, most avenues for cheap computer gear have been exhausted: Prime Days, eBay, even swapping gear in a parking lot. But there’s one place where you can find a true bargain: your local university campus. It’s weird, right? Tuition and housing costs are absolutely skyrocketing, but the humble computing shop on campus sells gear — collected from students moving out, faculty, and staff — and resells it for super cheap. What most people don’t realize is that those bargains are available to you, the public, as well as students already paying tens of thousands of dollars per year. Yes, this is indeed the era of the used PC, but there’s a better way to buy them than sketchy Facebook Marketplace meetups. Just don’t expect to buy any used primo gaming PC. These stores cater strictly to productivity buyers, which is why it’s the tip and the topic of this week’s Smart Mode newsletter. Welcome to PCWorld’s newsletter, Smart Mode! The focus of this newsletter is productivity: from software to hardware to peripherals, all with the idea to get what you need to get done, efficiently. I’m your host, Mark Hachman, covering the productivity tips, tools, and trends that you need to know about, both from within PCWorld and beyond. If you want the latest issue in your inbox each week, just sign up right here. A few weeks ago, I dropped off my son Aidan at his first year of school at UC Santa Cruz. (Go Fighting Banana Slugs!) We tried to nudge him toward some smart choices (you don’t need eight pairs of jeans, just wash them) and, of course, send with the tech gear I chose for his dorm room and backpack. Aidan prefers subdividing a widescreen monitor into two windows, so we brought his widescreen — or did we? Somehow we packed the van without the monitor ever making it inside. Uh-oh. What then? A run to Best Buy? Some frantic Amazon ordering? Nah. Just a quick trip to the UCSC Surplus Store, the best bargain bin for PC gear most people have never heard of. Inside what was once an old barn were rows of laptops, stocked casually on shelves. All-in-one iMacs and Apple displays. Bins of hard drives. It was all run by a genial older dude (this was Santa Cruz; he was a dude) who hooked us up and basically just offered us the run of the place. Were there prices? I guess? Not really. So we walked out of the store with a mouse, keyboard, large 1080p display, cables, and a random laptop power supply for $30. Honestly, I felt like I should have loaded up. Everyone knows what storage prices are going for right now, and there were just bins of hard drives available. I saw a 3TB 3.5-inch hard drive on top, an ideal addition to a hard-drive caddy to solve the storage crisis. I’m pretty sure that drive was like $20, but again…no prices that I could see. Everything was pretty much negotiable, where “negotiating” was already lower than I expected to pay, and where phrases like “I don’t know, let’s say [dollar amount]” were used pretty liberally. Campus surplus stores combine the value of bargain-bin shopping with the casual interaction of your local computer shop. That computer shop, though, has to pay rent and make a profit. Your local university is funded by its endowment and every student who is handed a diploma. The goal of the surplus store is generally little more than trying to keep its accumulated e-waste out of a landfill. It’s like visiting a Michelin restaurant, relatively; everyone else is lining up for the ten-course tasting menu. You’re just there for the breadsticks. What makes this tip worthwhile, I think, is that many people associate “campus computer shop” with “students only.” That’s often not the case, especially if the university in question is a public one. The public may have restricted hours, but you still can get access. Just keep in mind that each university operates on a campus-by-campus basis. UCSC has a used computer store; UCLA does not. Instead, it sells new laptops at “education discounts.” That’s great, but not really what we’re looking for. On the other hand, the University of Minnesota (listed below) collects so much that in the fall they simply give away things for free. Here’s a small list of possibilities. Be sure and check out the university, state school, or even community college near you. Who knows? - University of Washington, open 10-4 to the public every Tuesday. - UC San Diego: 10-3:30 Monday through Friday - University of Minnesota ReUse: Thursdays, 8:30-5, Saturdays, 10-4 - UT Austin: Thursdays, 3-7; Saturdays, 8-12 Bargain shoppers can often follow the surplus store on social media for new offers, like Penn State, below. The fact that the universities oversee the sales has a side benefit: they’re governed by data protection laws. Donate a laptop, and you can be fairly confident it will be wiped clean. Likewise, if you purchase a hard drive, you can be assured no malware is hanging out, ready to pounce. At least at UCSC, I was encouraged to just a grab a nearby laptop and some cable and double-check if the display worked. I like that vibe. (Just don’t expect a return policy. Once you’ve bought it, it’s generally yours.) I think it’s great that nerds of all stripes can come together and shop electronics swap meets and flea markets, or dig though online listings and government auctions for bargains. In Silicon Valley, however, everyone seems to know down to the dollar how much everything will cost. UCSC’s garage-sale atmosphere was casual, laid-back, where I was almost guaranteed a deal along with the chance that I might just find something amazing. I know I’ll stop by again. I’m somewhat ambivalent on the new RTX Spark platform from Nvidia. If you buy a laptop with 32GB of memory ($2,599?! Ouch!) it’s split between the CPU and the GPU. That also means that you don’t get offered the opportunity to run an agent like Hermes. It feels a bit like there’s a “base” and a “premium” experience within RTX Spark. - Right now, I have a review of the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra (32GB) and it’s a decent laptop, though with many aspects that will give you pause. I tested and tested and tested, so if you want to dive deep, please do. - If you want all of the interesting stuff (at least to me) pulled out and summarized, I have that as well: eight things I learned about the RTX Spark, and you should know, too. - Apps that slurp up data on the sly need to be rooted out. Google Gemini can be a culprit. - I’m still churning away on my Googlebook review, but here’s Ashley’s review of the HP Googlebook 14.I can see where she’s coming from… - Feels faster? That’s the claim some make whenever Microsoft issues a new update. And this one is literally aimed at speed. Productivity tip of the week: Shorten your meetings, automatically Everyone appreciates a little time at the end of a meeting to check email, use the restroom, or just do a little prep work for the next one. By default, however, meetings tend to be scheduled for the full hour. That doesn’t have to happen! In the Outlook settings menu, select Calendar from the left nav bar, then Events and invitations. Click the checkbox for “Shorten duration for all events” and simply select the appropriate shortened meeting duration. One click, and everyone on your team will love you. Or they should! Thanks for reading! Thanks for tuning in to this edition of Smart Mode, PCWorld’s newsletter devoted to helping you make the most of your life, smartly. Sign up and have it sent to your inbox every Thursday!

item.title: Your desk is a cable mess. These 9 gadgets will help tame it
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Your desk was probably clean at one point, with just a laptop and its charging cable as needed. Then came the monitor, the keyboard, the mouse. At some point you threw in a few wireless pads for your phone and other smaller accessories, and pretty soon it became a wild mess of cables that sprawl all over. You shoved it all behind your desk and tried to forget it. Maybe you tell yourself the web of cables is a necessary evil, but actually that’s not true. You can trim it down to almost nothing and make your desk clean and presentable once more, all without giving up anything. A few key upgrades can level up your setup and eliminate clutter. The trick isn’t to hide but to consolidate. The gadgets below will help you cut down on the cables, then route whatever’s left into organized spaces. If you want to tame your desk cable situation, this is how you’ll do it. Route all peripherals through one central hub This Anker Monitor Stand with USB-C Hub kills four birds with one stone. First, it’s a monitor stand—it raises your monitor to eye level for reduced eye strain while freeing up space underneath for light storage. Second, it’s a USB-C hub that accommodates several USB devices, HDMI, SD/microSD, Ethernet, 3.5mm audio, and passthrough charging routed to your laptop’s single USB-C port. Third, all of those connections are isolated to the monitor stand instead of huddled around your laptop and cluttering your desk space. Fourth, the stand has a cable shelf on its underside for coiling excess cable lengths. If you don’t need a monitor stand, a normal USB-C hub can still kill two of those four birds at a fraction of the price. The Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Hub routes many of the same connections (minus 3.5mm audio and one USB-A port) to your laptop, allowing you to tame a lot of that desk clutter. Route all peripherals through your monitor The 27-inch Dell Plus S2725DC is a monitor that doubles as a light USB-C hub. Don’t need a monitor stand and don’t want a separate gadget bringing its own clutter into the mix? This might be the way to go. It’s best if you don’t have a lot of peripherals—two USB-A ports are enough for a keyboard and mouse, plus one 65W USB-C to keep your laptop charged and one 15W USB-C for charging your phone or some other small accessory. Those USB-A ports can also be used for 5Gbps SSDs and flash drives in a pinch. The monitor itself is functional for office work, complete with a 1440p IPS display and refresh rate up to 144Hz. If you want to level it up, there are two higher-tier models: the 27-inch Dell Pro P2725QE with 4K/100Hz IPS, plus 90W of power delivery for your laptop and Ethernet; and the 27-inch Dell UltraSharp U2725QE with 4K/120Hz IPS, plus 140W Thunderbolt 4, more USB-C ports, and even KVM switching. Use one keyboard/mouse/monitor setup with two PCs If you’re like me, you have a single desk with two machines: a desktop PC and a laptop. What if you want to use the same set of keyboard, mouse, and monitors with both machines? Then you need a KVM switch, which is similar to a USB hub except it can connect to two separate machines and “switch” between them at the press of a button. The AV Access iDock P10 is a budget-friendly option that supports dual monitors via HDMi and DisplayPort, plus a few USB ports and an SD card slot. If you only have a single monitor, you can go even cheaper with the Ugreen HDMI KVM Switch, which supports up to 8K/60Hz. And if you only need switching capability for your peripherals but not your monitor, you can go even cheaper with the Ugreen USB Switch, which lets you share four non-video ports between two machines and switch on demand. A power strip with built-in retractable USB-C cables One of the best ways to declutter cables is to go retractable in as many places as you can. That way you only have to deal with messy cables when they’re actively being used. The Gitryin 12-in-1 Desktop Charging Station is one of my favorite charging solutions because it has four retractable USB-C cables, each reaching up to 33.5 inches at full length and delivering 65W of power when used individually. With a max throughput of 260W, it’s more than enough for power users and multi-user offices. You also get four extra USB-C ports along the front and four AC power outlets on the back, so it doubles as a power strip for your PC, monitors, and other non-USB-powered gadgets. Want to declutter your desk with a true all-in-one power station? This one’s hard to beat. If you have separate wireless charging pads for your Apple Watch, AirPods, and smartphone, then here’s a decluttering trick you’ll love: Belkin’s UltraCharge Pro is a 3-in-1 wireless charging station. It has a main pad for your AirPods, a side pad for your Apple Watch, and a 25W MagSafe pad for your phone. That MagSafe pad works with iPhones and Qi2-certified Android phones, and it can even keep your phone angled for easy spotting of notifications, doomscrolling, or even watching video. If you want to cut the price in half and you’re okay with some compromises, the Anker MagSafe Charging Station is almost the same except the phone pad only charges at 15W and doesn’t have an adjustable viewing angle. Ergonomic monitor control with cable channels You could buy cheap monitor arms, and they might even come with cable management features… but you get what you pay for. Cheaper arms often have flimsy clips that barely hold cables in place and warp over time. If you want sturdy arms that look great, route cleanly, and actually hide your cables out of sight, then Secretlab’s Magnus Monitor Arm is the one to beat. Its cable channels are spacious and heavy duty, with magnetic cable guides that conveniently snap on and off. The arm attaches securety using a C-clamp, compatible with any desk between 0.4 to 1.9 inches thick. Keep your remaining cables tidy and out of the way So you’ve reduced the number of cables on your desk as much as you can. With whatever remains, you’ll want to route them cleanly to eliminate as much visual and spatial clutter as possible. You could use cheap adhesive cable clips that come in packs of dozens, but you get what you pay for—they can snap, they don’t hold tightly, and they aren’t adjustable once placed. These Ugreen Cable Organizer Clips come in packs of six, they securely open and close using magnetic clasps, and they just look better. A mesh basket to contain disordered and messy cables It’s easy to clean up clutter on top of your desk. But what about below it and behind it? That’s where my biggest mess was, with an unkempt pile of cables shoved up against the wall. One solution is this Cinati Under-Desk Cable Tray, which is large enough to house a traditional power strip. Route your cables here and neatly store the excess within, keeping any mess out of sight. It clamps onto most desks using versatile C-clamps. Sleek desktop power routed cleanly through a grommet If your desk has a 3.15-inch grommet and you aren’t routing any cables through it, here’s one upgrade you should really consider: Uplift’s Pop-Up Power Grommet. It turns that grommet into a charging station with a 20W USB-C and double 18W USB-A ports. Need power outlets? You can “pop out” the grommet, which reveals four AC outlets as needed. When you’re done, pop it back in and keep your desk flush and clean. It’s a great way to turn any unused home office desk grommet functional.

item.title: Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% review: an awesome and affordable mechanical keyboard
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% impresses for a big brand's budget keyboard, proving a proper mechanical 'board for a song can be done when you put your mind to it. It looks good and feels excellent with tactile switches and a surprisingly sturdy plastic chassis. If I'm being nitpicky, the lack of any adjustable feet and more basic software customisation are sore misses, but on the whole, this is a highly impressive mechanical board. - -ABS keycaps have the potential to get quite shiny - -No flip-out feet feels like a missed feature Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Razer Reclusa X Mini 65%: two-minute review Razer has a long and storied history when it comes to its own mechanical keyboards, but at virtually every opportunity, it has charged a bit of a premium for them. Even the more enthusiast-focused ones, such as the BlackWidow V4 75%, have tended to transplant the brand's gaming look onto a hot-swappable, sound-dampened board with a premium price to match. The Reclusa X Mini 65% takes a different approach. At $49.99/£59.99/AU$99.95, it's aimed squarely at the budget end of the market, and at people who might be buying their first mechanical keyboard, which is a good market to go after. The problem a first-time buyer has is simply the breadth of choice on offer, and it can be very daunting to pick a keyboard, even if I think it's simpler than the internet wants you to think. Likewise, a lot of the choices on offer tend to skimp on certain things, or they aren't offering a complete package – Razer has hit the nail on the head when it comes to the fundamentals of a good affordable mechanical keyboard. For instance, the plastic chassis is compact but has a surprising amount of heft, and I couldn't find any real deck flex. For the money, that's a pleasant surprise. Moreover, the third-gen Orange tactile switches are the best Razer has made in a while, with a pleasant feel under finger that kept me using this keyboard long after the review period was up, and the mint green colorway is a departure from the brand's usually quite aggressive, gamer-centric styling. It's only really the little things that let it down. I'll continue to bemoan the presence of ABS keycaps, even on a more affordable keyboard, and the lack of any form of adjustable feet on the underside feels like an oversight. The absence of any wireless connectivity may not please some, but I don't necessarily see it as a big issue given the price. Even so, the Reclusa X Mini 65% is a very easy keyboard to like. It's sturdy, smooth to type on, and looks the part, and it has room to grow if you want to experiment with different switches, being hot-swappable and all. It's a fantastic first mechanical keyboard for a lot of folks, and all the more fun being from a brand I might not have expected to get it so right. As much as the Reclusa X Mini 65% isn't an expensive keyboard, it doesn't exactly feel like a bargain-bin product, either. Far too often, cheaper keyboards from brands up and down the reputational ladder are plastic fantastic, with corners that flex and a chassis that feels like it'll give up as soon as you put your fingers down to type. Not so with this product. The plastic chassis may be compact, but it has a surprising amount of heft and no real deck flex, which I'm delighted about. I first got hands-on with this product at Gamescom 2026, and the first thing I did was pick it up, try to flex the chassis, and was met with resistance from the keyboard's frame, which genuinely surprised me. That doesn't happen too often these days. The style Razer has opted for with this keyboard is also unlike any of its previous efforts. The brand's other keyboards, even the more enthusiast-focused ones such as the BlackWidow V4 75%, simply transplanted the signature look of its gaming products and supplemented it with hot-swappable switches, sound dampening, and so on. The Reclusa X Mini 65% actually looks a little more like a product that someone getting into mechanical keyboards might want to purchase. I'm a particular fan of the keycap styling and color options with the mint green accents for Esc, Return, the Space Bar, and arrow keys, plus white for other function keys. The main alphanumerics are black with the same green hue for the legends. Being doubleshot is nice for durability, too, although I will continue to nag Razer about its use of the shiny ABS plastics. Even at the more affordable end of the market, we're seeing the more durable (and much more shine-resistant) PBT used more often, so it would have been nice to see it here. The 65% layout is largely okay to use day-to-day, and provides you with some of the functionality of bigger footprint keyboards, such as a single column nav cluster and arrow keys in the corner. Other functions, such as the F-row, media playback and controlling the keyboard's RGB backlighting, are relegated to a function layer. I'd prefer a bigger layout, but 65% is the absolute smallest I can get away with using day-to-day without feeling hemmed in. The interface around the back is nice and simple, with just a USB-C port for hooking the keyboard up to a PC or Mac. After all, it is just wired, with no other connectivity options available – for the price, it's perfectly fine. I do have another bone to pick, though. The underside has no adjustable feet. While the default rake of the Reclusa X Mini 65% is comfortable enough for me, it's a shame that you can't tilt it any further up. Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% review: Performance - Tactile Gen 3 Orange switches feel solid under finger - Decent acoustics and customisation potential - Bright RGB lighting and convenient software on offer One of my bigger keyboard-related axes to grind has often been Razer's own switches. The older Green and Yellow switches never did anything for me compared to other options out there, and the third-gen Orange soft tactiles that's been fitted to my sample of the Reclusa X Mini 65% have been Razer's pick of the bunch for some time. These are 50g switches, providing a slightly heavier press than your typical crop of linears, with a little more weight under finger than I usually like. There's a decent tactile bump halfway down the keypress to boot. For typing an array of articles with this keyboard, this review included, it's been nothing if not agreeable. The switches also come pre-lubricated, meaning they’ve had a small dab of lubricant on the stem, switch housing, and elsewhere inside for a smoother keystroke. The idea of lubricating switches has become more tied to the modern mechanical keyboard hobby in the main, and it works to the Oranges’ advantage by offering a smooth keystroke that’s nicely interrupted by the soft tactile bump halfway down the keystroke. If these switches aren't your jam, though, then the Reclusa X Mini 65% is hot-swappable and compatible with your usual MX-style three- or five-pin switches, and it works the way you'd expect, with no soldering or funny business required. That said, I couldn't spot a keycap or switch puller in the box, so you'll need to supply your own if you want to swap them out. Doing so is easy enough, though, so you can change switches in a matter of minutes, potentially changing the feel of the keyboard completely. For instance, I had some Cherry MX Northern Lights knocking around, which are a lighter and much quieter linear switch, which changed the feel of the 'board completely. Regarding noise, this Razer keyboard isn't the quietest, and when you get up to speed, it can be quite loud. That said, there is internal dampening to help reduce any case rattle and ping, and the acoustics on offer here are largely pleasant, with a crisp and quite bright sound when you get into the groove. Software duties are handled by Razer's Synapse 4 suite, which is a major improvement on the older and clunkier forms of Synapse that came before it. As expected for a keyboard that isn't packed to the rafters with HE or TMR or whatever else, the customisation here is largely limited to key remapping on two layers, plus enabling the brand's Snap Tap feature for unusually brisk side-to-side movement in the likes of CS:2 and configuring the keyboard's RGB lighting. The Reclusa X Mini 65%'s solid keycaps mean the Chroma lighting this keyboard has is more of an underglow than a full-blown Pink Floyd gig, although it's still plenty bright enough and works well with the aesthetic of the keyboard. Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% review: Price & release date Razer launched the Reclusa X Mini 65% in September 2026. At $49.99 / £59.99 / AU$99.95, it's easily one of the most affordable keyboards the brand has ever released, let alone an enthusiast-focused one. That price puts it firmly in entry-level territory. It's much cheaper than the Razer BlackWidow V4 75%, which sits in the more enthusiast-focused part of Razer's range, and it takes on the likes of the MechLands Vibe99, another budget board that trades a premium finish for strong value. It also sits alongside Gamakay's TK75 V2, which proved you don't need to spend big to get a satisfying typing feel. What sets the Reclusa X Mini 65% apart from a lot of these more affordable mechanical boards is how much it gets right for the money. The solid chassis, hot-swappable switches and doubleshot keycaps are rarely found together at this price, and when they are found together, it can usually mean a compromise on feel, one way or another. The compromises are a wired-only connection, 1,000Hz polling and shiny ABS keycaps, but for most buyers on a budget they're easy to forgive. Should I buy the Razer Reclusa X Mini 65%? The Reclusa X Mini 65% has a surprising amount of heft for the money, with no noticeable deck flex. That makes it feel a good deal more expensive than it actually is. You want a satisfying tactile switch under finger Razer's Gen 3 Orange switches are the best it has made in a while. The pre-lubed 50g stems and soft tactile bump make for a smooth, agreeable typing feel, and they're a pleasure for long writing sessions. This is a USB-C wired board and nothing else. That's perfectly fine for the money, but if you want Bluetooth or a 2.4GHz receiver, you'll need to look at other options. It might seem a small nitpick, but the lack of any flip-out feet on the underside of this keyboard can be a shame if you want to get properly comfortable with this board, hindering its ergonomics a bit. Synapse 4 is a big improvement on older versions, but you're limited to key remapping on two layers: Snap Tap and RGB control. If you want more tuning options, you'll need to look elsewhere. The MechLands Vibe99 goes after the same budget-minded buyer, and it's a solid performer, with well-lubed linear switches and a snappy response. It's a less handsome package than the Razer, though: the chassis feels solid but not premium, the retro styling doesn't charm, and the software isn't as good as it should be. It also uses a near-full-size 1800 layout rather than a 65% one, which suits you better if you want more keys. If you'd rather have a 75% layout, the Gamakay TK75 V2 is a lovely alternative, with damped switches that are great for typing and gaming and near-silent in use. That's a big contrast with the Razer, which can get loud once you pick up speed. The catch is that it lacks gaming-specific tweaks, so it suits typists better than players who want the likes of Snap Tap. How I tested the Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% - Used for gaming and productivity across Windows and macOS - A decade of experience as a journalist and mechanical keyboard hobbyist I tested the Reclusa X Mini 65% for around two weeks, using it as my main keyboard for work and play during this time with both Windows and macOS. I used it for typing up thousands of words a day with my PC and hooked it up to my MacBook Pro over Bluetooth as my primary keyboard for work, too, to judge its performance. I also used the Razer Synapse 4 software on Windows to remap keys, program the macros and see what else it had to offer. I've been a tech journalist for the best part of a decade, and have reviewed plenty of keyboards in that time from brands big and small. I'm also a mechanical keyboard enthusiast, so I have a keen eye for peripherals and have been involved with the hobby before it hit the mainstream.

item.title: ‘The run ends in the centre of this beautiful village’: readers’ favourite small ski resorts in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Bad Gastein is a relatively unknown gem. The Austrian state it sits in, Salzburg, offers free local transport (the guest mobility ticket) if you are staying in the state, so you can travel to the resort via train for nothing. The slopes are directly next to the station, too.
Puy-Saint-Vincent in France is a wonderful, small, child-friendly resort. Our grandchildren learned to ski each morning with great instructors on the gentle slopes under amazing azure skies. Three generations then made memories of a lifetime, skiing the wide quiet slopes together each afternoon. We enjoyed dog sleds and cosy hot chocolate in the slopeside cafes. A wonderful trip.
A historic railway and superb skiing in Norway Gausta, Norway, is such fun. Stay at Gaustablikk, the hotel built by Kirk Douglasâs stuntman, a wonderfully quirky piece of local history. Explore Vemork, the historic heavy-water plant where British and Norwegian resistance fighters carried out their daring sabotage during the second world war. For families, the on-piste skiing is friendly and accessible; while the cross-country trails are simply stunning. Then thereâs the real adventure: an old US military train climbs Gaustatoppen, opening up spectacular off-piste skiing with views and terrain that rival much of mainland Europe. Itâs a brilliant mix of history, skiing, scenery and adventure, and somehow remains a wonderfully under-the-radar destination.
Markets and gluhwein in the Austrian Tirol As a family of four, we loved St Johann in Tirol. Itâs a comfortable Austrian village with Christmas markets, picturesque churches and gorgeous frozen valley walks â with little marmosets and weasels to look out for along the river. Wherever you stay, you can walk to a gondola. Itâs really near to Salzburg airport, too. In Austria, kids get all-day lessons, which is a big bonus. Parents can just kick back or wander around and have a gluhwein or two. Prices were very reasonable in the Christmas holidays.
A localsâ favourite on the Italian border Tarvisio-Monte Lussari on the Italian-Slovenian border covers 24km (15 miles) of skiable terrain interconnected across two main sectors: the historic and stunning Monte Lussari pilgrimage peak and the Priesnig area. Used by local people and those in the know, it offers sufficient ski runs and good value ski passes and restaurants, and is much cheaper than neighbouring resorts in Austria.

Strap on a pair of randonnÃ©e skis and you can use the lifts to access spectacular backcountry skiing in the SunnmÃ¸re Alps. The views down to the fjord make this truly special. Pistes are illuminated for evening skiing.
A charming village in Les Trois VallÃ©es Saint-Martin-de-Belleville, in the French Alps (Les Trois VallÃ©es), is low at about 1,500 metres, so go mid-season. item.title: 17 Stylish, Woodsy-Chic Catskills Airbnbs for Every Season
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
As a lifelong New Yorker, the Catskills have been my go-to escape from New York City for as long as I can remember, and Iâve yet to run out of reasons to return to the Airbnbs in the area. There are ski towns that come alive with the first snowfall, Main Streets lined with antique shops and old-school diners, and miles of mountain roads that (somehow) turn even more lovely when the leaves change color. Just a couple of hours north of the city, this four-county region of southeastern New York has been luring urbanites into the mountains for centuries. In the 19th century, grand resorts drew vacationers seeking fresh air and scenery; later, the Catskills were known for their summer camps and folk music, with the southern region earning the nickname the Borscht Belt for its collection of hotels, stays, and camps that welcomed Jewish travelers who often faced antisemitism at other American resorts. Today, that storied past mingles with a new generation of creative small towns, farm-to-table restaurants, and design-minded hideaways that make a weekend away feel like a proper change of pace. Finding the right Airbnb in the Catskills is almost as fun as the actual visit: Across the region, you'll find glass-walled A-frames tucked into the forest, renovated farmhouses with room for the whole family, and modern cabins where the wood-burning stoves practically beg you to cancel your dinner plans. Some are minutes from hiking trails, swimming holes, and ski slopes; others put you close to beloved towns like Woodstock, Phoenicia, and Tannersville. Whatever the season, these Catskills vacation rentals make a wonderful starting point for your next upstate adventure. Read on for 17 of the most beloved, top-rated, and still-bookable Airbnbs in the Catskills, per a city gal who's already added them all to her wishlist. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. Our top picks: - Best for an editor-approved stay in Phoenicia: Lush upstate tree house - Best for proximity to a charming main street: Walkable carriage house in Woodstock Why we love it: Pool and hot tub, firepit, mountain views, kid-friendly amenities, barbecue, hammockA beautifully restored 1920s Catskills cabin set on four private acres, this home is all vintage charm and modern comforts. Located just minutes from top destinationsâseven to Phoenicia, 10 to Belleayre, and under 40 to Hunter and Windhamâitâs a perfect year-round base for skiing, tubing, hiking, fishing, exploring swimming holes, and beyond. Inside, enjoy open-concept living with a gas fireplace, four cozy bedrooms (each with memory foam beds, USB ports, and sound machines), and a fully equipped kitchen with coffee, spices, and cooking tools. Outdoors, thereâs no shortage of ways to unwind: A seasonal saltwater pool (open May through September) set behind the house offers mountain views and comes with towels, umbrellas, sunscreen, and pool toys. The six-person hot tub is available year-round and sits just off the back doorâideal for a morning soak or evening under the stars. Youâll also find a hammock, a firepit, outdoor blankets, and plenty of games and books for cozy days in. Town: Shandaken Things to do nearby: Panther Mountain Trail, Phoenicia Diner, Woodstock Brewery, The Pines, Belleayre Ski Center, Shandaken Inn, Hunter Mountain Why we love it: Mountain views, free parking on premises, sound system with extensive record collection and DVDsBest for larger groups or families, this colorful rental fits up to eight guests. The charming 1950s cabin is perched atop Rose Mountain and set on five private acres with sweeping views of Slide Mountain and access to a creek. Its mountaintop location lends a feel of total seclusion, yet guests are just 10 minutes from Belleayre Mountain and less than an hour from all sorts of hip restaurants, fun bars, and cool main streets. With retro â70s style and modern amenities, the Rose Mountain House features three cozy bedrooms (all with Casper or Leesa mattresses), two full baths, and a well-equipped kitchen ideal for cooking up local fare. Relax indoors by one of two wood-burning stoves or on the screened-in porch with sweeping mountain views. Or, enjoy the spacious yard for games and an alfresco meal around the firepit, hammock, and picnic table. For analogue travelers, the house also boasts an extensive record collection, DVDs, VHS, and board games. Just a short drive from Phoenicia, Margaretville, and top Catskills ski resorts like Hunter and Windham, this is a great base for folks traveling in any season. Town: Big Indian Things to do nearby: Rochester Hollow Trailhead, town of Pine Hill, Belleayre Mountain, Shandaken Wild Forest Why we love it: Garden view; bathtub; in-unit washer and dryer; large outdoor space with a hammock, barbecue, and sun loungersIn the heart of the Central Catskills, this property is just 10 minutes from Belleayre and within reach of Hunter, Windham, and Plattekill. Perfect for family getaways or friend reunions, the spacious cedar-clad chalet boasts a chefâs kitchen with a five-burner gas range, large fridge with an ice maker, and heated floors throughout. The open living area is filled with natural light, thanks to its four skylights, while the cast-iron, wood-burning stove adds warmth to chilly nights. Unwind on one of two large decks or share stories around the firepit out back on the sprawling lawn. The home is surrounded by woods, ensuring plenty of privacy and peace. Inside, enjoy streaming services, a Bluetooth speaker, and a range of board games and puzzles for laid-back evenings. With three comfortable bedroomsâtwo queen bedrooms and a king suite with a private balcony, workspace, and Herman Miller ergonomic chairâitâs perfect for rest and relaxation after a day in the mountains. Whether youâre lounging with a book, cooking up a feast, or venturing out into the surrounding nature, this might just be the base for your next adventure. Town: Shandaken Things to do nearby: Glenbrook Park, Esopus Creek, Belleayre Ski Resort, Tremper Mountain, Phoenicia and Phoenicia Diner Why we love it: Fully stocked kitchen, plush memory foam beds with percale bedding, speedy Wi-Fi, streaming television, air conditioning, garden and mountain viewsNestled on eight acres in the heart of Catskill State Park, this Airbnb (named Camp Vista Falls) is a conveniently located creekside cabin with panoramic mountain views. The 120-year-old home has been thoughtfully restored to offer a soulful retreat, thanks to its playful mix of rustic charm and sleek amenities primed for your comfort. Tucked just minutes from Phoenicia, Mt. Tremper, Woodstock, and some of the best hikes, restaurants, and breweries in the area, itâs the perfect year-round escape for outdoor enthusiasts and those seeking an excuse to simply relax. You'll find vintage furniture, curated art, and a collection of books, board games, and puzzles inside, creating a homey vibe. Whether you're warming up by the fire after a day on the slopes, preparing a meal in the quaint yet well-equipped kitchen, or simply sipping on a coffee at sunrise on the porch, this cabin is an ideal place for respite. Need even more incentive? The hosts offer a 15% discount on stays of seven days or more, and an additional 10% off for early bookingsâso plan ahead and stay a while. Town: Shandaken Things to do nearby: Timber Lake Camp, Halcott Mountain, The Clubhouse at Shandaken Inn, Shandaken Historical Museum, Big Indian Park Why we love it: Private water access; indoor fireplace; board games; private backyard with a barbecue, hammock, and outdoor dining areaTucked just a short drive from Woodstock and the iconic Phoenicia Diner, this private cabinâvisited in 2025 by Traveler commerce director Madison Flagerâoffers a tried-and-true Catskills retreat. Surrounded by lush forest and a serene creek, the space feels like your very own woodsy, secluded oasis. Enjoy lazy days lounging in the hammock by the water, or curl up inside where cozy decor and calming vibes create a perfect escape. The tree houseâstyle spot is impeccably clean, with soft towels and comfy beds that make relaxation effortless. According to Flager, the cabin would make a lovely spot for a reading retreat or a couple's weekend. If you come as a group, there are plenty of ways to stay entertained nearby or at home: A few classic board games sit on a shelf in the living room, and out back, you can grill meals, sit around the table with a deck of cards, or make s'mores by the campfire. Without exaggeration, there are a half dozen different seating options in the backyard, from the hammock strung between two sky-high trees to the cushy loungers on the deck to the camp chairs positioned in front of the second firepit. Town: Phoenicia Things to do nearby: Simpson Ski Slope, Woodstock Brewing, Phoenicia Diner, Sleepy Hollow Campground, Romer Mountain Trailhead, Rail Explorers: Catskills Division Why we love it: Waterfront spot with river views, backyard with hammock and barbecue, fully equipped kitchen, indoor gas fireplace, Marshall Bluetooth sound systemJust a 15-minute drive from the charming and quintessential town of Livingston Manor, this peaceful cabin can comfortably host up to four guests. With floor-to-ceiling windows and sliding doors that overlook the private backyardâas well as views of the forest out of the large bedroom windows (especially the primary)âthe creekside propertyâs design is thoughtful, with a modern and airy open concept throughout. A picture-perfect indoor fireplace turns on with the touch of a button and is best enjoyed with some board games and tunes on the sound system. The deck includes a Weber grill to throw some patties on, a dining table to enjoy them at, and an outdoor couch for lounging with your crew. Further in the backyard, find a hammock and a creekside firepit surrounded by nature. Itâs a quick drive to many of the Catskillsâ buzziest restaurants and art galleriesâand without traffic, the site is less than two hours from NYC. Not to mention, the home is tucked right next to Willowemoc, a tiny hamlet filled with charming creeks and brooks. This is the birthplace of fly-fishing in the USâon the nearby Beaverkill River and the Fir Brookâwhich lie just outside the home. Town: Livingston Manor Things to do nearby: The DeBruce (with its award-winning tasting menu), Willowemoc, Long Pond Trailhead, Roscoe Why we love it: River and garden views, wood-burning fireplace, Google Bluetooth sound system, board games, reading materialWhether heading on a weekend getaway or an extended stay, this Scandinavian designâinspired cabin is dream-like for those in search of a tastefully restored yet historic gem. Tucked on a scenic, rural road, guests will find themselves in a setting that is not only picturesque but perfect for disconnecting and cozying up by the fireplace with a glass of wine. Less than a five-minute drive from the town of Hamden, itâs easy to come across a good cup of coffee, locally sourced groceries, antique shops, and hiking trails if you so choose. When staying in, relax in Adirondack chairs alongside the crackling firepit and babbling stream. Or, barbecue on the charcoal grill with fresh meats or trout from the local butcher. Thoughâwith only one bedroom plus a sofa bed in the living roomâit's probably best for two, not four, as the listing suggests it can fit. Town: Walton Things to do nearby: Hamden, West Branch Nature Reserve, Brushland Eating House, Historic Hamden Covered Bridge Why we love it: In-unit washer and dryer; fireplace; pizza oven; waterfront location; backyard with hot tub, sauna, firepit, and barbecue; king bedTucked in East Jewett, a scenic and low-key hamlet in Greene County (part of Catskill Park), this unique cabin mixes modern comforts with a romantic, rustic charm. Why am I personally adding this base to my upstate bucket list? The fairy taleâesque fireplace setup in the living room. And, of course, the chance to bake pizza in the pizza oven, have loads of fun in the game room, take a dip in the hot tub, and relax in the wood-fired sauna. While thereâs much to do nearbyâfrom trailheads and hiking paths to swanky cocktails in Tannersville, a town just north of the propertyâyou might find it difficult to leave this stylish oasis. Town: East Jewett Things to do nearby: Colgate Lake, Hunter Mountain, Tannersville, Mountain Top Arboretum, Deer Mountain Inn (for upscale fireside dinners), Hotel Lilien (for cocktails, a pool table, and the occasional live band) Why we love it: Washer and dryer in-unit, record player, indoor fireplace, board games, private backyard with a barbecue and firepitNestled beside a quiet brook, this two-bedroom home (one king and one queen) is a design and nature lover's paradise. Thoughtfully curated as a blend of comfort and culture, guests can expect to be surrounded by vintage finds, fun textiles, and art collected from the hostsâ journeys abroad. Whether you're checking in as a small family, two couples traveling together, or a friend groupârest assured, if you're booking this bad boy, it's safe to say you have good taste. It's all very intentional, from the warm and inviting interiors to the fireside loungingâwhile the spacious deck makes outdoor moments that much more magical. Town: Livingston Manor Things to do nearby: Catskill Brewery, The Kaatskeller, Main Street Farm, Old Souls, Drooz, Dette Flies Why we love it: Mountain views, private sauna, hot tub, firepit, wood-burning stove, record player, board games, kid- and pet-friendly amenitiesNestled in the ever-evolving western Catskills, Roscoe is a charming mountain town known as Trout Town USA for its world-class fly-fishing. This Airbnbâset on a private hillside with beautiful mountain viewsâis a spacious base with curated interiors, warm wood accents, unique architectural details, and lots of space to gather with the people you love. The living room is home to a wood-burning stove and soaring ceilings, as well as a separate loft level with cozy seating and a smart TV, ideal for movie nights. On the main floor sit three comfortable bedrooms, a full bathroom, and walkout patio access to the great outdoors. Town: Roscoe Things to do nearby: Courtyard Restaurant, Catskill Fly Fishing Center & Museum, Willowemock, Livingston Manor FAQ: What's the best town or region to stay in the Catskills? There's no âbestâ town in the Catskills, but there's certainly some to keep on your radar, depending on your preferences. To the north, towns like Hudson, Catskill, and Tivoli skew artsy and architectural, where design galleries sit beside unfussy yet thoughtful restaurants. To the west, Woodstock and Phoenicia thrum with trailheads, river bends, vintage shops, and old-school diners. Further into the mountains, Shandaken and Big Indian are known for their sense of seclusion and access to natureâfavorites of hikers, writers, and anyone looking to go quiet for a while. item.title: 15 Best Hotels in the Dolomites, Italy's Charming Mountain Region
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
In winter, a snowglobe scene of dusted pine forests and glittering frozen lakes surrounds the best hotels in the Dolomites. It thaws just in time for summerâs âthe hills are aliveâ buttercup meadows and lush valleys, all surrounded by perfect peaks. Indeed, the Dolomites mountain range is maddeningly beautiful, a cinematic landscape dotted with storybook chalet towns and villagesâit's just one reason the region received its moment in the spotlight during 2026âs Winter Olympics. Visitors will notice the Dolomites remain deeply rooted in Ladin culture and traditions, with Roman and Milanese weekenders setting a palpably Italian (not touristy) tone despite the area's rising popularity. Ready to stay and see the fairy tale with your own eyes? From restrained eco-boutiques with easy access to the slopes to spa stalwarts with steaming outdoor pools tipping over pastoral valleys, the best hotels in the Dolomites offer year-round appeal. Read on for our editors' favorites. Our top picks: - Read Full ReviewNature dictates everything at this CO2-neutral A-list hideaway in the Italian Dolomites. The site was chosen for its abundant sunshine, spring water, mountain air, and views of the jagged Odle massif, which is framed by picture windows in all 62 minimalist suites. The landscape is also woven into the biophilic architecture, Celtic wellness rituals, and intricate âforest cuisine.â After hiking or skiing in the Plose mountains, guests can recharge over a tasting menu in the amphitheater restaurant as the sun sets with all the drama of Mount Doom. The history of the complex is similarly dramatic: It was conceived in 1912 as a sanatorium for Austro-Hungarian aristocrats but lay dormant for years. For its relaunch in 2020, Stefan and Teresa Hinteregger added three 12-story towers and an astonishing spa with a swim-in, swim-out pool. A villa for 10 followed in December 2024, and a concept restaurant, Yera, which celebrates the fruits of the forest around a firepit in a cave, arrived in June 2025. âLisa Johnson - Read Full ReviewThis cliffside-hugging, glass-fronted forest retreat has an Instagram-famous pool thatâs framed by the Dolomitesâ famous peaks. But better yet, itâs a beautiful hotel designed to celebrate the region's shifting seasons. The mix of guests ranges from trendy couples lounging in dressing gowns on a spa break to outdoorsy types wearing messy boots and young families with grandparents in tow on the hunt for some truly fresh air. Book a guided forest bathing walk to meander slowly through the woods and fully immerse yourself in nature. Back at the hotel, the heated onsen pool etched into the cliff face is the perfect spot to relax, while the larger infinity pool is made for taking in sweeping views of the valley below. There are 47 rooms in six different categories, all of which face jaw-dropping mountain views. Cozier rooms in the main house sleep up to four and benefit from easy access to the pool, restaurants, and bar. Alternatively, there are three houses 985 feet away. I was driven to one in a Miramonti-branded vehicle, where I entered through our own garage. A private elevator opens to reveal an open-plan living space, interiors crafted from natural materials, and light-wood walls that still emit their earthy scent. Bespoke, custom-made furniture and decor pepper the space and prove the precision is in the details. âSophie Knight - Read Full ReviewLocated in the heart of the Dolomites on the Alpe di Siusiâthe highest Alpine plateau in Europeâthe ski-in, ski-out location offers direct access to the pistes in the winter, and South Tyrolâs flower-flecked network of hiking and biking trails in the summer. As youâd expect from the brand, wellness is at its core, with a health-forward treatment menu on offer, plus hearty Tyrolean and Italian fareâas well as excellent Alto Adige winesâfor those who donât want to hold back. All of the wood-clad, cozy rooms face the slopes and have a balcony or terrace. Sauna is a serious operation here, with herbal and Finnish saunas, salt and aroma steams, and a convivial outdoor seating area in the snow where half-clad spa-goers chatter. In summer, the hotel offers multiple activities including biking, hiking, climbing, trail running, paragliding, zip-lining, wild swimming, and helicopter rides. âJemima Sissons - Read Full ReviewSet high above the South Tyrolean valley, Hotel Saltus is a design-led sanctuary immersed in forest and mountain views. This family-run retreat lives and breathes its surroundings, with chic contemporary minimalism that lets the views do the talking. Rooms are calm, expansive, and built to frame the ever-changing landscape, while the food celebrates local ingredients with a refined, modern twist. Wellness is at the heart of the experience, from the serene Forest Spa to guided forest bathing sessions that encourage guests to slow down and reconnect, both with themselves and with the earth. Whether youâre here to hike through the breathtaking Dolomites or simply switch off, Saltus offers a deeply restorative stay where time stretches and allows you to lean into the art of doing nothing. I expected to return home feeling more relaxed, but I was surprised to find myself returning with a little bit of Hotel Saltus lodged in my heart forever. âLucy Bruton - Read Full ReviewOf all the chic new hotels that have opened in the Dolomites in recent years, Castel Badiaâset in a manor house that dates back to the year 1000âis at the top of the pile. The hotel, an Alpine counterpart to ÂPugliaâs Borgo Egnazia, was created by Ian Schragerâs protÃ©gÃ© Aldo Melpignano, who brings a new sense of cool to high-end Italian hospitality. The building has served as a courthouse, a convent, a private castle, and, since the 1970s, a hotel. A recent renovation saved everything that could be saved: The floors, wood ceilings, stuccoed vaults, and frescoes remain. Silence reigns in this ancient castle, where life, as it did in the Middle Ages, revolves around the courtyard. Through that nexus, you access the garden, swimming pool, guest rooms (there are 28 in total, along with a three-story chalet), basement spa with frescoed relaxation rooms overlooking the mountains, and the crypt of San Lorenzo, a protected site that, like the rest of the castle, is open to the public. This remains a sacred place, even as guests enjoy its sybaritic offerings. âSara Magro - Read Full ReviewAt the foot of the Alpe di Siusi, the highest alpine pasture in Europe, Sensoria Dolomites sits low, nestled beside a river in a South Tyrolean village. This is an adults-only all-inclusive retreat where rooms are minimalist, making way for maximalist views via large windows and wraparound balconies. Days ideally begin with a dip in the heated pool, with steam rising as the Dolomite peaks sharpen into view, or with a relaxing sound meditation in the spa before breakfast at Anima restaurant. From here, itâs a five-minute stroll to the cable car. In summer, a short ascent delivers you straight onto rolling alpine pasture; in winter, locals wander aboard with skis slung casually over their shoulders, bound for the wide, sunlit slopes. âNoo Saro-Wiwa - Read Full ReviewAdler Balance was built in 2008 right next to its sister property, Adler Dolomiti, and the structure was created to blend harmoniously into the Alpine landscape. Unlike Adler Dolomiti, Adler Balance is adults-only and has a particular focus on wellness. The hotel has evolved into a highly specialized destination medical spa, combining a five-star hotel experience with longevity programs led by a team of doctors, therapists, and wellness experts. Nestled in a peaceful corner of the Dolomites, it offers a retreat from the crowds that have started to flock here year-round. Large and comfortable rooms, attentive staff, and an elegant dining scene are all present, but it's the hotel's mountain heritage, as well as its picture-perfect location, that's the main event. âAlessia Armenise - Read Full ReviewNestled in the LÃ¼sen valley at the foot of the Dolomites, LÃ¼snerhof Naturhotel is the kind of place youâd let your mind wander to when dreaming of peace and tranquility. Escaping the city for a weekend here feels close to medicinal. The well-being offering is bespoke and holistic, championing regional produce as well as the skills of specialist practitioners who visit for a week at a time to share their craft. Each of the hotel's 59 rooms is cleverly designed to optimize its surroundings and spotlight the location, no matter the season. Interiors reflect the Alpine setting and integrate years-old Dolomite rock, Swiss stone pine, and a clay finish on the walls. Fresh mountain water awaits guests in their roomsâa small but location-centric touch. The spa here is huge, and home to the longest sauna trail in the Alps. Practices take place in immersive outdoor locations, including the forest sauna, floating salt grotto, natural bathing pond, whirlpools, and infrared gondola. âAlice Morey - Read Full ReviewDuring my three-hour drive from Milan to Madonna di Campiglio, the landscape shifted from Call Me By Your Name to a real-life vintage ski poster. Adamello Brenta Nature Park, which surrounds the area, was beautiful enough to spark emotions as we drove past tumbling waterfalls and turquoise lakes, where the mountainsâ reflections are as awe-inspiring as the peaks themselves. When we pulled up to Casa Cook Madonna, we were delighted to see our neighbors were a chocolatier, a local cheese shop, an ancient little stone church, and the base of the gondola, from where cable cars serenely floated up the mountain, which we watched from our roomâs reading nook. Each of the 50 rooms can be summed up as contemporary, cozy, and intimate, and modern in a way that truly magnifies the surrounding environment. Think earthy stone surfaces, deep woods, and sleek modern headboards juxtaposed with the kind of rustic, wooly blankets that would fit nicely into Ralph Laurenâs Colorado ranch. Being at the base of the slopes, youâre in a prime position to ski. âTamara Southward - Read Full ReviewIt's hard not to be awestruck when you catch your first glimpse of this hotelâit resembles a magnificent spaceship, its stark rectangular silhouette appearing to levitate above the treetops, illuminated from beneath and casting an enchanting glow that creates the illusion of hovering. The vision is the work of owner Markus Huber, a native of Brixen, and Gerhard Tauber, who designed the contemporary tree house concept, the largest of its kind in Europe. Perched on lofty 115-foot stilts resembling tree trunks, My Arborâwhich fittingly means âmy treeâ in Latinâis a tree house that's strictly for grown-ups, attracting a health-conscious, sociable, and energetic crowd seeking adventure and relaxation in equal measure. The location is equally a knockout, set in stunning surroundings with direct access to the Plose ski area from right outside the hotel. After days out hiking or on the slopes, the spa is the ultimate relaxation spot, spanning 27,000 square feet over two floors, and comprising saunas, a Turkish steam room, an icy plunge pool, and a large panoramic outdoor hot tub with incredible views over the valley. âKarin Mueller - Read Full ReviewYou can sense a unique vibe at San Sonnea Family Dolomitesâa family-friendly wellness, farm, and ski hotelâwhen you first arrive. Perhaps itâs down to the mutual understanding shared by all the adults-with-hangers-on here. It's a place for parents who want to enjoy the finer things and locations in life, no matter how many boundary-pushing blow-ups their toddlers or teens may have in store, such as the slopes of the Dolomites, organic fine dining and drinking, and luxurious but eco-friendly design and decor. Fortunately, the many creative activities on offer in the phenomenal kids and babies clubs are likely to stop oncoming tantrums in their tracks, from pony rides and alpaca petting to finding their own breakfast eggs at the little farm and taking part in productions in the huge theater. Access to a 2,900-foot-long slope and lift comes included, with private ski lessons easily arranged for those ages two-and-a-half and up. Besides the food and drinks, the property's very highest highlight is its five pools, including a shallow option with a cinema screen, one with speedy slides, and an indoor-outdoor heated pool from which steam wafts, ideally situated for swimmers to marvel at the snow-capped mountains nearby, or firepit come nightfall. âBecky Lucas - Read Full ReviewSince 1939, Rosa Alpina has been a firm favorite with the high-altitude summer crowd for its Alpine classicism and San Cassiano location. Then Aman took the mantle in 2003, and its Ladin roots (once a farm and inn) were thrust through the groupâs contemporary prism: the hallmark clean lines, subdued hues, and angular furniture. Rather than end three generations of stewardship, Aman kept the Pizzinini family firmly at the helm, respecting their hotelier pedigree and, ultimately, preserving something no amount of glass, steel, blonde woods or Michelin stars can buy: soul. Long-time Aman collaborator, Jean-Michel Gathy, rolled up his sleeves and integrated the notion of Alpine coziness into Amanâs famously restrained aesthetic with clever lighting, milky fabrics reflecting the surrounding pine forests and snow-capped peaks, and abundant cubic fireplaces warming the pared-down rooms. Guests can paraglide, whoosh down the endless runs forming the Dolomiti Superski area, gallop through the fragrant pine forests on horseback, or simply take a remedial walk through the UNESCO-listed landscape with its crisp, lung-cleansing air. And with Amanâs finely tuned spa and excellent food at The Grill, thereâs always something worth trudging back to base for. âMaddalena Fossati - Read Full ReviewTo soak up illustrious glamour, head to the pearl of the Dolomites, Cortina dâAmpezzo, where youâre likely to splurge most of your budget on oysters and Champagne. But thereâs a reason why this northern gem, located only two hours away from Venice, has become a favorite among Italians and was the host of the 2026 Winter Olympics. Around the area, youâll find a handful of beautiful lakes, including Lago di Misurina and, slightly further, Lago di Braies. The perfect base for your adventures is Rosapetra, whose secluded location on the outskirts of Cortina offers a low-key, relaxing few days. Rosapetra is an Alpine cottage where each of the 33 rooms looks out towards the Dolomites. From a well-equipped gym to a wellness circuit of iced waterfalls, saunas, and a 39-foot swimming pool, youâll have everything you need to warm up or restore your muscles pre- and post-ski. âLucrezia Worthington FAQ: How we choose the best hotels in the Dolomites Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a CondÃ© Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.
