Source: Condé Nast Traveler
One common misconception about cocktail bars in Milan is that the cityâs drinking culture begins and ends with the aperitivo. Yes, the pre-dinner ritual still defines much of the cityâs social culture, but the bar scene in Milan has evolved significantly over the past few years, thanks to a brigade of hospitality-minded, boundary-pushing talent. While the Spritz and the Negroni Sbagliato arenât going anywhere anytime soon, a new wave of mixologists has elaborated on the customary red-orange palette, pouring an array of jewel-toned beverages layered with technique, seasonality and innovation. Some of these cocktail bars in Milan are part of larger operations with restaurants; others distinguish themselves independently. From the classic to the new, here are 18 of the best cocktail bars in Milan where even teetotalers will drink exceptionally well. Reservations are recommended whenever possible. Like its equally multi-faceted sibling Moebius (named after the French cartoonist), Lubna claims a namesake: a radical Italian comic book heroine of the 1970s. It arrived on the scene in December 2024 inside a former tram depot in the district dubbed SouPra (âSouth of Pradaââthe Foundation, that is). The vast, faintly industrial open warehouse incorporates concrete and wood surfaces, and glass walls frame views of the al fresco crowd in the courtyard. The layout splits between a restaurant and a cocktail bar, with a listening lounge tucked into the back corner, whose walls come alive with flickering anime cartoons. The cocktails echo executive chef Enrico Croattiâs flame-driven cooking, incorporating ingredients grilled or charred over open fire. The Strawberry and Roasted Capsicum is a smoky riff on a Negroni, built from mezcal and diluted juice from a roasted pepper, while a spin on the tequila-based Toreador adds yoghurt and house-made âblack oilâ infused with fiery charcoal ember. Rita, Edoardo Nono and Chiara Buzziâs modern classic opened in 2002 along the Naviglio Grandeâwell before the banks of the canal-crossed district evolved into the bar-loaded hotbed it is today. Nono and his team pioneered practices now considered commonplace, such as house-made infusions and juices and buffet-free quality aperitivo eats served at the table. Sit at the U-shaped Larchwood bar backed by a bottle rack displaying over 500 premium labels that stretch to the ceiling, or plop yourself on one of the red banquettes edging the walls. Among the ever-changing, inventive cocktails is one retro throwback: the Gin Zen, a 90s-style hodgepodge of crushed ice, gin, muddled fresh ginger, lime, and soda that Nonoâs been mixing since day one. Just across the street is Ritaâs Tiki Room, which opened in 2019. This epic institution evokes the charm of a bygone era while still setting the benchmark for cool. Avail yourself of a Negroni Sbagliato, or the âMistaken Negroniâ swapping prosecco for gin, created in 1972 by late owner Mirko Stocchetto. Better yet, ask for âuno Sbagliato grandeâ which swims among clinking ice cubes in a glass goblet bigger than your head. If youâre not in the mood for bitter, Bar Bassoâs plentiful cocktail list runs 500 long and counting. The clientele represents all walks of life: young and old, regulars and newbies, locals and travellers. Stocchettoâs son Maurizio, the current owner, marked the 50th anniversary with a light refurbishment but one that kept the vintage backbone intact, from the brocades and mirrors to the marble floor and dark wood panels. The crowds can spill onto the sidewalk any given evening (especially during Design Week), so make sure to book in advance for prime-time imbibing. Bob The Other Side is the newest venture from Luca and Michele Hu, the twin brothers behind the Chinese Box Group and longtime stalwarts of Milanâs mixology scene. The name is literal: the bar is just beside Bob Milano, their cult Isola cocktail spot, hidden behind an unassuming teal door that recalls the entryways of old Milanese tenements. Step inside, though, and the mood shifts entirely. The design plays with geometry, reflection and depthâthink warm wood panelling, bronzed mirrors, walnut tables, brass accents and luminous geometric details, including a striking hexagonal counter. Cesar Araujo, who also leads the cocktail program at Bob, crafts the drinks, which include the Hidden Love with gin, tomatoâpomegranate cordial, and Timut pepper; Ray of Illusions, blending pisco, sherry, black sesame and apple-flavoured matcha; and Holy Water, a lush mix of Woodford Bourbon, spiced honey, citrus and coconut milk infused with Lapsang. Donât be alarmed by Camparinoâs proximity to the Duomoâthereâs nothing tourist-trappy about this 110-year-old mainstay. At the ground-floor Bar di Passo, sip Campari classics at the counter, surrounded by an exquisite Art Deco backdrop that has captivated patrons since its opening. In the upstairs Sala Spiritello, Tommaso Cecca and his bar team push boundaries with creative cocktail pairings. The current menu, crafted in honour of Camparinoâs 110th anniversary, traces Camparinoâs history through 12 drinks, starting in 1915, then marking the start of each subsequent decade through 2025. Among them: Italian Blood (1935), with Campari, tomato water and aromatic herbs; Lacto Garibaldi (1975), which combines Campari with lacto-fermented orange juice; and the Breeze (1995), a vibrant blend of Campari, vodka, pomegranate juice, zallotti blossom, and pink grapefruit soda. At the intimate, reservations-only Sala Gaspare, named for Campariâs founder, the drinks reimagine the aromas and ingredients that make up his iconic bitter. Occupying a 700-square-metre former textile warehouse, Moebius juggles multiple concepts, one of which is a cocktail bar that currently ranks seventh on the Worldâs 50 Best Bars list. Bar manager Giovanni Allario weaves unexpected twists into classics, like the Pesto Martini with vodka, white balsamic vinegar, and homemade pesto and a Gremolada Negroni with notes of lemon and parsley. The decor juxtaposes its iron-flecked industrial skeleton with warm and natural accents like a 700-year-old Andalusian olive tree. A backlit concrete bottle rack extends three metres high from behind a light wood counter that seats seven, while wood tables and couches and chairs in earthy grey, brown, and blue hues speckle the boundless venue. Donât let the name fool you â Dario Cominiâs trailblazing molecular mixology mecca is about as far from a British sports pub as it gets. The elaborate, experiential drinks are presented on trays or pedestals alongside clever fixings. The French Kiss rests beside illuminated lips, clutching an aphrodisiac flower, and patrons put the finishing touches on the signature C.S.I. cocktail with syringes and test tubes. A dark wood bar salvaged from New Yorkâs Knickerbocker Hotel anchors the room from its post in front of shelves crammed with over 1800 bottles. Dozens of eclectic objects, like stone buddhas and African masks, that Comini procured from his travels, complete the treasure trove look. No reservations, no exceptions. Ever. Thereâs always a line, but itâs worth the wait. If you get there around 10-15 minutes before it opens, you should be able to get seated during the first turn. Named after a former Futurist magazine, Lacerba opened in 1999 and strikes the perfect balance between nostalgic and zany: vintage ads and abstract art adorn the walls, dozens of empty bottles dangle from the ceiling, an illuminated cutout of Milanâs Duomo twinkles beside shelves stocked with analogue clocks and travel books â an ambience that can dub as an icebreaker if youâre struggling for conversation on, say, a first date. Though, Lacerbaâs always a blast with friends and loved ones. Of owner Angelo Trapassoâs 51 cocktails, five change monthly â a sure bet year round is the Discorso aritmetico alla fidanzata (Arithmetic Speech to the Girlfriend), a riff on the classic Americano. Lacerbaâs famous Bloody Mary menu features ten recipes ranging from classic to playful, like the flowery Saint Mary in Love with dry sherry and elderflower liqueur. Luca Marcellinâs 26-seat cocktail bar couples the conviviality of a neighborhood place with the intrigue of a speakeasy. You ring a bell to enter, but the mystery isnât so much whatâs inside as the windowed facade reveals a lively, chatty crowd, but rather in the curiously clever cocktails, like the Negroni allâavocado, which incorporates their own avocado oil distillate or the Sazerac Fire, mixed with Cognac, cocoa beans and chilli pepper, and hazelnut bitter. Gin and tonic lovers can choose from five versions. Drinc.different, which Marcellin co-owns with Desiree Brunet, is just five minutes from its sibling. The narrow, 18-seat nook feels equally inviting but more discreet with low tables and chairs and dim lightingâperfect for date night. The equally curious drinks include NâDoritos with Doritos-infused Pisco, red vermouth, and chocolate bitter, and the refreshing FraâPaloma with tequila, cinnamon, citric, grapefruit soda, and a house-infused strawberry and vanilla mezcal. NiccolÃ² Caramiello and Stefano Rolloâs bar in Lambrate evokes âOld Milanâ with its sleek green Guatemalan marble bar top and custom-made furnishings procured from recycled materials, lived-in walls, and dark wood floors. Absinthe is the star of the glass here, with 11 Italian, Swiss, and French labels on offer, appearing in reworked classics like the Absinthe Marini, Absinthe Rita, Absinthe Mule, and Absinthe Julep. For an alternative to the anise-flavoured liqueur, try the Million Dollar Hotel made with vodka, port, mastiha, beets, and a hint of wasabi. Provisions include tinned Spanish and Portuguese fish and French oystersâitâs not unusual for the latter to appear in a martini. Earlier this year, the team opened Cactus Joe, a cocktail bar focused on agave distillates. Whoâs Norah? Accounts may vary, but the one consistency is that sheâs a figment of the ownersâ imagination. An anagram for âCasual Ristorante Cocktailsâ, Carico also means âpoweredâ in Italian, a fitting pun to a concept packing punchiness and prowess. Domenico Carella oversees a selection of cutting-edge drinks, like the Capsicum Funky, with tequila, white chocolate, jalapeÃ±o, and citrus; Arantius Siesta, a mix of mezcal, sherry, orange, and sesame; and the Chipotloni, a negroni kicked up with Chipotle. Canât decide? Opt for the mini cocktail route: four half-portions for 30â¬, or stick to reliable staples like a gin and tonicâwith over two dozen types of gin to choose from. The kitchen delivers playful, elevated small plates, such as a croque monsieur with mortadella and Parmigiano fonduta, and pulled pork tacos, among others. Every so often, the seven-seat Negroni Room pops up for an experiential, all-sensory food-and-drink experience dedicated to its namesake legendâbook your spot in advance. Carella is also one of the forces behind Ultra, a pizzeria and cocktail bar that opened last year. The Bulgari Hotelâs swanky bar area centres around a glossy, oval black resin island that seats 20 and rests beside a glass wall looking out at the garden. Bar manager Patrick Greco and his team update the menu twice a year, and on the list today are a half-dozen evocatively named creations. The Polaris dazzles with tequila, mezcal, blackberry syrup, and a touch of citrus air foam, while the Hydra balances gin, mastiha, carrot, celery, and a bright, zesty twist of lime. For a deeper dive, the Belvedere Martini Experience presents two scaled-down Belvedere-based martinis side by side to illustrate the subtle contrasts in flavour, aroma, and texture. When the weather cooperates, book an al fresco table among the pagoda trees and boxwoods of the lush garden that feels light years away from the city. The eighth floor of Casa Brera, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Milan, houses one of the cityâs most stunning rooftop venues: Etereo, a sky bar and restaurant whose spectacular 360-degree panorama of the city encompasses the Duomo, Galleria, Castello Sforzesco and the Porta Nuova skyscrapers. The space feels both vintage and contemporary, decorated in shades of cherry red, brown sugar and desert sand, with windowed walls, cane-backed chairs and lacquered tables, all anchored around a red arabesque marble bar. The âArt of the Aperitivoâ cocktail list features 13 signature drinks, each paying tribute to a different Milanese neighbourhood. The BellâArt Martini, an ode to the Brera, combines vodka, gin and white penja and is finished with a spritz of black pepper, while the Heritage draws inspiration from Castello Sforzesco and Corso Sempione, mixing tequila, mezcal, mastiha, tonic, angostura bitters, Champagne, passion fruit, and a touch of green mandarin. The first cocktail bar in Milan from Flavio Angiolilloâs now epic Farmily Group, MAG Cafe, opened in the heart of the Navigli in 2011. The cocktail current roster, named âWorld Comes to Milanâ, features a selection of cleverly crafted cocktails, each named after a different country, in honour of the 2026 Winter Olympics. China combines ginseng rum, litchi liqueur, rice-and-peach cordial, sapsang souchong tea and lime, while France mixes Cognac Martell VS, prickly pear distillate, Ratatrip (a proprietary take on French ratafia), ratatouille water, wine-tomato reduction and lemon. The boho-vintage interior ups the charm factor: an Argentine pharmacy counter, dangling bicycle wheels affixed with lights resembling the spokes of a ship helm, and ever-changing paintings and ornaments. The groupâs other establishments include La Pusterla, MAGâs sibling; 1930, the elusive invite-only speakeasy; Backdoor 43, the worldâs smallest bar; Iter, a cocktail bar equipped with a proper kitchen; and two outposts of Tripstillery, Italyâs first cocktail bar with a distillery onsite. In Milanese dialect, âTusaâ means âgirlâ, the inspiration for owner Norma Galdamezâs cocktails, all named after 20th-century female trailblazers. The Sissi combines rum, lime and chestnut honey, with notes of coffee and mint, for a tipple as intense, sweet and unpredictable as its namesake princess. Gin, cardamom, Lapsang, Verjus and pink grapefruit soda channel the vivacious spirit of the late Raffaella Carra, an iconic, boundary-breaking Italian entertainer, while the Ella Fitzgerald, with Jameson Black Barrel, toasted sesame, Shochu, toasted hazelnut and rakomelo reduction, is warm, velvety and elegantâjust like her voice. The inviting, feels-like-home ambience is enhanced with low velvet sofas in shades of green, blue, and yellow, marble and wood tables, and quirky gold-framed artwork and portraits on the sapphire walls. At the Mandarin Oriental, Milan's chic retreat, beloved local barman Guglielmo Miriello has crafted a cocktail menu inspired by far-off lands like the Majorelle with eucalyptus-infused vodka, Acqua Bianca liqueur, blue spirulina, Moroccan lemon cordial, and mint bitters, and the Port Elizabeth, with almond-infused cognac, rooibos and honeybush shrub, hibiscus water, and sherry. Sit indoors among the sleek black and white marble interiors or, weather permitting, head outside to the garden nestled into the courtyard outfitted with pastel armchairs and sofas among the climbing ivy and leafy potted plants. Gestoâs dining room, brightened by Michela Picchiâs pop art, carries a hint of speakeasy intrigue, with a short passage leading to the listening bar, or Sala Malinconia (Melancholy Room), concealed behind a mustard-yellow curtain. In Italian, malinconia evokes a softer, more nostalgic feeling than pure sadness, an appropriate descriptor as the room evokes the good days of the analogue era. Emerald-green walls display framed vintage prints, while guests gather around candlelit dark-wood mid-century-style furnishings. At the front, a turntable rests in a wooden wall unit lined with more than a thousand vinyls, its central mirror tilted down to reflect the DJâs hands at work. The cocktail list gives new life to classics, like the Boogie Mary with butter-and-sage-infused Grey Goose; the San Carlo, a Negroni spiced with pink pepper; and the Matcha Amor, a gimlet-style blend of mezcal, coconut cream, lime, matcha and white chocolate. A tapas menu lets you easily turn your evening of cocktails into a fully-fledged dinner. A version of this story originally appeared on CondÃ© Nast Traveller UK.

Source: Condé Nast Traveler
You just canât argue with that Disney magic. Whether youâre a Disney adult or a begrudging occasional visitor, at some point throughout the day, a little bit of Disney dust will hit you. Maybe itâs the fireworks, or the rides, or the many, many Disney-shaped food items. If not that, it might be seeing the excitement on kidsâ faces when they run into a princess, Avenger, or cartoon character IRL. Iâm no Disney evangelist, but I would say that if you canât have fun at a theme park, consider looking inward. (And okay, as a former resident of both California and Florida, I have spent more than my fair share of time at the parks on both coasts.) All that aside, trips to the parks are expensive, so if youâre here to find ways to save, I get itâbelow, find all the current discounts and promotions to be aware of before planning your next trip to Disneyland. Disneyland discounts for Magic Key holders For the uninitiated, annual passholders are called Magic Key holders, and they can pop in and out of Disneyland as they please (with some terms and conditions in there). Through December 15, these theme park enthusiasts can save up to 15% on select Standard and Premium room types at premium Disneyland Resort hotels. The offer is tailored to Sunday through Thursday night stays at Disneyâs Grand Californian Hotel & Spa, Disneyland Hotel, The Villas at Disneyland Hotel, and Pixar Place Hotel. Of note, you must present a valid active Magic Key pass at check-in to secure the discounted rate. If you're headed to Hawaii, passholders can save even more, with up to 35% off select stays at Aulani Resort in HawaiÊ»i that take place between October 19 and December 23, 2026 (with checkout no later than December 24). Those staying five or more consecutive nights can take 35% off; for those staying four consecutive nights, 30%. Disneyland discounts for military members Savings are available on an ongoing basis for active-duty and retired US military personnel, including the National Guard, Reservists, the US Coast Guard, the US Space Force, the Commissioned Corps of the Public Health Service (PHS), and the Commissioned Corps of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Tickets start at $98 for kids of these travelers and $104 for adults purchasing a one-day, one-park ticket. These tickets may not be combined with other ticket discounts or promotions, and cannot be sold or transferred. While going to the parks for just one day is the most cost-effective option, your per-day cost does go down when you opt for multi-day tickets instead. For example, a one-day ticket will run you between $104 and $224 based on the date you select. If you go for two days, your price per day starts at $168; for three days, it drops to $142 and up per day; for four days, from $120 per day; and for five days, from $104 per day. A few things to note: Disneyland is much smaller than Disney World, with just two parks, so it is possible to cover a good amount of ground in a single day. However, especially if youâre coming from out of town, you may want a few days there so thereâs less pressure to squeeze every ride and meal into a single day. Thereâs also the question of purchasing one-park-per-day tickets or upgrading to a Park Hopper ticket (an extra $100 per day). If youâre visiting for just one day, Iâd suggest the Park Hopper ticket so you get to experience both parks. For multi-day trips, it really comes down to preference; youâll want to decide between chunking out your park visits or having the freedom to roam back and forth between parks throughout the day (which, size-wise, is definitely doable). Save on food, merchandise, and add-ons with Disneyland discounts beyond tickets Tickets are one thing, but once youâre inside the park, itâs easy to rack up charges on dining, souvenirs, and add-on experiences. If youâre concerned about sticking to a budget, there are a few surefire ways to cut costs. For one, take a look at the gift card section next time you're at Target, Costco, or Samâs Club, as they sometimes sell discounted Disney Gift Cards. If youâre interested in an additional credit card, new Disney Inspire Visa Card holders can earn up to $500 in the form of a $300 eGift to spend at the park and a $200 statement credit after you spend $1,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. Youâll also earn Disney Rewards Dollars on all card purchases, including: - 10% on card purchases made directly with Disney+, Hulu, and Stream.ESPN.com - 3% on card purchases at gas stations and most Disney US locations - 2% on card purchases at grocery stores and restaurants When it comes to food, placing mobile orders via the Disneyland App can help you track food spending more easily and find quick options in place of more expensive sit-down meals. Lastly, consider dining off-property or at Downtown Disney to curb costs. On my last visit to Disneyland, I stayed right across the street from the entrance at Park Vue Innâthe proximity was amazing, and it had a pool and hot tub. Rates start at $229 a night, and rooms with kitchenettes are available, which make coming back midday to prep meals a breeze. item.title: Best Christmas bars London: 11 perfect places for festive cheer
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
A mulled wine snatched in Covent Garden market will always be welcome, but sometimes Christmas calls for more. Meeting old friends? You probably want somewhere you can sink into. Need a break from shopping? Bubbles and a cloakroom are suddenly your non-negotiables. Happily, the streets of London are lined with such chic and cosy retreats – and some of the very best come into their own each December. This is the month of the year when a 276-year-old pub in Kensington will entirely cover itself in conifers, when a single tree in the lobby of the city’s most storied hotel becomes the talk of the town, and when the idea of a whisky bar in Soho never feels more right. So, from grand drinks palaces in Mayfair to candlelit cocktail bars on Dickensian side streets, these are the places I love for Christmas cocktails and festive drinks. Some are gloriously classic and others are excitingly contemporary, but they each share something essential: they will hit the spot whether you’re in the midst of a shopping day or at the beginning of a night out. What is the most famous Christmas bar in London? A London institution and a year-round fount of next-level hospitality, Claridge’s isn’t just for Christmas – but it does feel extra special at this time of year. With its designer Christmas tree, the storied hotel pulls out all the stops, making its bar one of our favourite places for a festive drink. What is the most Christmassy pub in London? Think of London at Christmas and it might even be one of the city’s legendary pubs that springs to mind – probably in a timeless scene of cosy corners, crackling log fires and warming drinks. For the effort it makes with its decorations – inside and out – the Churchill Arms in Kensington gets our vote for the most festive atmosphere in town. Where is the most Christmassy place in London? With its seasonal theatre productions, festive markets and late-night shopping, Covent Garden has a strong claim to be London’s most Christmassy neighbourhood. At the centre of the celebrations is Miracle on Russell Street. This pop-up cocktail bar from the cool Experimental Group has a new location for 2026, but the unparalleled levels of Christmas kitsch remain firmly in place. What are the best bars in London for Christmas? As ever, Londoners in search of a festive bar are spoilt for choice this year. Whether you’re looking for a hot new opening that’s celebrating its first Christmas or a timeless classic for a more traditional kind of evening, the city is teeming with options. We’ve gathered all of our favourites for you right here. Claridge’s goes all out at Christmas – and it’s a wonderful place for you to do the same. The reveal of the hotel’s Christmas tree in its lobby, which is created by a different designer or fashion house each year, has become one of London’s great advent traditions. Last year’s tree was designed by Burberry and 2026’s name is set to be revealed soon. Whoever it is, at some point in December, everyone should pop in and see it for themselves. From the tree, you’re just a few short steps away from the Art Deco Claridge’s Bar and the pretty-in-pink Painter’s Room. Take your pick – the hotel’s heady festive atmosphere permeates them both. Address: Brook Street, Mayfair, London W1K 4HR With its voluptuous planters and hanging baskets, the Churchill Arms has become an icon of Instagram. Behind the colourful exterior lies some similarly overstuffed interiors – and a real pub. Come December, the floral arrangements outside are replaced by dozens of Christmas trees and hundreds of thousands of lights. The switch-on is an event that should be seen at least once, but whenever you’re shopping on High Street Ken or soaking up Notting Hill’s festive atmosphere this year, the Churchill is worth dropping into. Address: 119 Kensington Church Street, Kensington, London W8 7LN Miracle on Russell Street, Covent Garden For 20 years, the Experimental Group has built its reputation creating handsome hotels and elegantly restrained cocktail bars in Paris, New York and London. Each December, though, it gives elegant restraint a month off. In its place, it opens Miracle – a Christmas-themed pop-up that used to sit within Covent Garden’s Henrietta hotel, but for 2026 is taking over a bigger space on nearby Russell Street. The décor will be indescribably kitsch, but the drinks will be sophisticated – the Christmapolitan features vodka, elderflower, Carpano dry vermouth, spiced cranberry sauce, lime, rosemary and absinthe mist. Address: 9 Russell Street, Covent Garden, London WC2B 5HZ On a cobbled alley, in a row of 19th-century workshops, the Umbrella Workshop flickers with Dickensian atmosphere. Step inside and you will find a tiny, often candlelit bar that is, in some ways, deeply contemporary. A sort of test kitchen for more famous siblings like Bethnal Green’s Sun Tavern and Spitalfields’ Discount Suit Company, this is where the group’s talented cocktail team soft launch their latest creations. Behind the fun names (‘Hong Kong Ping Pong’, ‘Do Not Redeem’) lie some seriously inventive drinks – last Christmas there was a gorgeous Ginger Old Fashioned. On account of its size and popularity among the city’s cocktail cognoscenti, this is definitely one to book ahead. Address: 10 Cleeve Workshops, Boundary Street, Shoreditch, London E2 7JD On a Mayfair shopping spree, the foodie enclave of Bruton Place is always worth keeping in mind. A couple of doors down from the Guinea Grill, Brutes is a 2026 opening with real pedigree behind it. Founders James Stevenson and Guy Mazuch met while working for JKS (the influential group behind restaurants from Gymkhana to Legado). Martinis, caviar, crisps and gildas – their new place hits a number of trends that have defined the London scene this year. The martini menu is front and centre: tick the boxes to choose your spirit, your style (dry to dirty) and your garnish (Monster Munch, anyone?). For a novel pick-me-up, you might prefer the G.O.A.T (olive oil vodka, espresso, goat’s whey penny lick and miso). The classical stylings of this long, thin and low-slung newcomer will make you forget this is its first Christmas. Address: 34a Bruton Place, Mayfair, London W1J 6NR You might have noticed that Sloane Street has had a glow-up. It fully reopened just in time for last Christmas, when it made a splash with a golden canopy of lights. At the end of the street, close to where Ralph Lauren has started doing festive pop-up stores, sits Martino’s. This is where Martin Kuczmarski (of Mayfair favourite The Dover) pays homage to mid-century Milanese trattorias. Amid the wood-panelled walls and dark terrazzo floor, there’s a glamorous bar offering refined takes on aperitivo hour classics. Italians do it better – it’s a rule that holds for Christmas, and a seat here would be a wonderful gift to yourself and a friend. Address: 37 Sloane Square, Chelsea, London, SW1W 8AN If December puts you in the mood for whisky, Milroy’s is where to indulge yourself. Brothers Jack and Wallace Milroy opened it as a specialist whisky shop on Greek Street in 1964, and it still sells bottles today – useful if there’s a whisky lover on your list. But this is also a bar. There’s a copper-topped counter in the shop for drams, and at the back, a bookcase swings open onto a staircase down to the Vault, a candlelit cocktail bar that hosts jazz nights on Mondays – the perfect soundtrack for one of the bar’s signature coconut butter old fashioneds. Address: 3 Greek Street, Soho, London W1D 4NX Trafalgar Square always has its tree from Norway, but it’s the lights of Regent Street that truly feel like the centrepiece of Christmas in London. Just off the famous shopping street, Sketch is a destination that always deserves a detour. Each year this Georgian townhouse embraces a different festive theme. Last year’s was ‘The Art of Après’, with snow falling at the entrance and even the much-admired pod loos getting a makeover. The Parlour, its playful all-day café and bar, is the spot for mulled wine and winter warmers after a shopping run. On Saturday nights, it turned into a full après-ski party, with DJs and champagne. We’re looking forward to seeing what this year’s theme is. Address: 9 Conduit Street, Mayfair, London W1S 2XG At the heart of this handsome hotel bar in Holborn is an open fire in a showpiece hearth. That’s enough to sell us on it, but there’s more. Named after the cartoonist whose caricatures adorn its walls, Scarfes Bar feels like the drawing room of a gentleman’s club, with plenty of places to sit soft. Or you could take a seat at the long bar. Either way, you’ll be well placed to explore a widely acclaimed cocktail list featuring some elegant seasonal specials. For further festivities, the Rosewood always has a pop-up Christmas cocktail terrace in its courtyard. Address: 252 High Holborn, Holborn, London WC1V 7EN Sprawling in the basement of the One Hundred Shoreditch hotel, Seed Library is a low-lit and low-slung bar with warming touches of 1970s design. The retro approach extends to the entertainment – DJs only spin vinyl – and a drinks list overseen by the great Ryan Chetiyawardana. Last Christmas, the man you might know as Mr Lyan signed off on a Pine Clover Club of Renais gin, raspberry juice, pine propolis (courtesy of Bermondsey Street Bees) and lemon. Open until 2am at weekends, everything here is set up for a group looking to go late in the run-up to 25th December. If you find yourself in and around the festivities on the South Bank this year, remember Ryan also has Lyaness in Sea Containers House for an elevated pitstop. Address: 100 Shoreditch High Street, Shoreditch, London E1 6JQ To call the Fat Badger a pub is to undersell it. First of all, you have to find it – look for a side door with a small badger sign. Climb the stairs and you’ll find a dim, wood-panelled bar. The real surprise and delight, though, is the lineup of entertainment. On any given evening, there will almost certainly be live music – full bands are squeezed in at weekends – and, if not, it’s only because it’s comedy night. Both would be great fuel for a Twixmas meetup. A floor above, there’s a small dining room serving a set menu of old-school British classics. Start with drinks and you might find yourselves sticking in the building for a while. Just the other side of the Westway, the Pelican is also part of Public House group – with more space and the same fire-lit atmosphere. Address: 310 Portobello Road, Notting Hill, London W10 5TA

item.title: Packable jackets: 17 that will fit in your carry-on
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Packing jackets can be tricky. They take up premium suitcase space, which means you can usually only afford to pack one or two per trip. The ones you do choose need to be versatile enough for whatever is on your itinerary, whether that’s dinner in town or a city walking tour. The best packable jackets are also insulated enough to keep you warm without being so bulky that they take up all the room in your bag. Does such a jacket even exist? After years of testing dozens of options on my travels – from downpours in Vietnam to hiking past waterfalls in Iceland and nights out in New York City – I can confirm there are at least a few good ones out there. If you’re searching for a jacket that really earns its spot in your carry-on, taking up as little space and weight as possible, I’ve got you covered. Whether you need an insulated puffer, a raincoat, or a dressier day-to-evening jacket, there's a lightweight option below that will keep you warm and dry this season. Even better, some of the best packable jackets fold down into their own carrying case. FAQ: What's the best way to pack a jacket? For jackets that don’t fold into themselves or their own carrying case, consider using compression packing cubes to remove excess air, making them even more compact. Without packing cubes, the best method for packing a jacket is to zip it up and lay it completely flat, fold both sides in by a third, fold the sleeves down on top of that, roll tightly, and tuck it into its own hood if there is one. Will a packable jacket actually keep you warm? Yes – if you pick the right fabric, a packable jacket will keep you comfortable even in frosty temperatures. Look for insulated options with down-like PrimaLoft, and an outer shell made of ripstop nylon (light but windproof), or recycled polyester that’s durable and quick-drying. A durable water-repellent (DWR) coating can also help to keep the weather out and the warmth in. What's the best type of jacket for travel? It depends on your trip. Are you getting active or hiking? You can’t go wrong with a puffer jacket that keeps you warm and protected from the elements. Are you travelling to a city? You’ll want a bomber, denim jacket, or cropped trench that’s functional but stylish. Simply put, the best jackets are ones that serve multiple purposes and are lightweight and water-resistant. item.title: Top spooky spots to visit for Halloween in San Diego
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
From the Haunted Hotel in Olivenhain to the Haunts of Balboa Park to the Scare Trail in El Cajon, there are a slew of scary places to visit for Halloween throughout San Diego County. Here are some of the top spooky spots. Sip & Scare Train rides: The Campo Railroad Museum will run Sip & Scare Trains for adults over age 21 at 6 p.m. Saturdays through Oct. 31. The train ride includes a journey through the haunted attraction, The Lost Train of Dr. Deadtrack, and entrance to the Karnevil afterparty, featuring live music, food, drinks and vendors. Tickets are $49.95-$64.95. Reserve at psrm.org/sipnscare. “A Haunting in Venice”: Halloween-themed gondola cruises start at 4 p.m. Oct. 28-31, run by The Gondola Company. The 50-minute gondola rides through the canals of Coronado Cays feature phantom gondoliers, soft organ music and spooky vibes. Rates start at $139. Visit gondolacompany.com/a-haunting-in-venice-cruise. Scare Trail: The Haunted Amusement Park’s mile-long “scare trail” features a haunted manor, spinning vortex tunnel, graveyard and witch’s cottage along with a rollercoaster creeper, spider’s cave and 3-D black light bumper cars, among other spooky attractions. Tickets are $25-$35. Opens at 7 p.m. Fridays through Sundays and certain other days through Nov. 1. Not recommended for children under 10; children 5 and under not admitted. Closed shoes required. Visit scaretrail.com. Haunted Hotel: The historic grounds of the Olivenhain Meeting Hall will be transformed into a Haunted Hotel from 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. Oct. 23 and 5:30 to 9 p.m. on Oct. 24 and Oct. 30 at 423 Rancho Santa Fe Road. New this year is Candy Mystery Trail and Monster Hunt. There will be spooky scenes ranging from a Haunted Swamp, Dr. Frankenstein’s laboratory and a Witches’ Lair to a Candy Mystery Trail. Actors are Scouts ages 11 to 17. There will be a carnival with prizes, live entertainment, crafts and food. Admission is free. Tickets for Haunted Hotel tour are $8 at the door. Additional costs for concession, carnival, and candy mystery trail. The event is a fundraiser for Scout Troop 2000. For questions, email troop2kcommunityoutreach@gmail.com. Visit facebook.com/HauntedHotel2. Haunted Harvest: Festivities include haunted house, carnival games, food, costume contest and farm animals along with beer garden, music and dance and magic show. The Haunted Harvest is from 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. Oct. 23-24 at The Heritage Ranch, 450 Quail Gardens Drive. Entry is $10; $5 for kids. Visit olivenhainfarms.com/haunted-harvest. Fall Festival: Haunted house, arts & crafts, face painting and food from 4 to 7 p.m. Oct. 22 at Del Lago Academy, 1740 Scenic Trail Way. The Haunted Forest: Half-mile Halloween Walk from 6:30 to 9:30 p.m. Fridays to Sundays through Nov. 1 in Ghost Town Banner City’s Haunted Forest at the historic Banner Ranch, 36342 CA-78. The old orchard area is decorated with graveyards, ghosts and ghouls. Costumes encouraged. Parental discretion advised because of “light gory scenes.” Admission is $13-$15. Visit bannerranchjulian.com. Headless horseman: A costume parade led by the headless horseman from the Poway Rodeo kicks off the Halloween festivities from 3:30 to 8:30 p.m. Oct. 24 at Old Poway Park, 14134 Midland Road. There will be a haunted house, carnival games and train rides until 8:30 p.m. A Nightmare before Christmas-themed area will be in the boxcar lot. Trunk or Treat is cohosted by the Poway Chamber. Admission to the haunted house, which is also open from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. Oct. 25-30, is $1 (not recommended for kids under age 5). A Halloween movie, “Hocus Pocus 2,” will be shown at sunset Oct. 25 near the Haunted House. Visit poway.org/Halloween. Haunts of Balboa Park: The scary experience features two haunts at Balboa Park: the mile-long Haunted Trail winding through the old twisted oak trees of historic Marston Point and Experiment Maze. Open select nights through Nov. 1 at Balboa Drive and Juniper Road. Advance tickets are recommended because there is a nightly capacity limit. Timed general admission stats at $34.99. Visit hauntedtrail.net. Howl-O-Scream: The “sinister” nighttime Halloween event at SeaWorld for mature audiences (separately ticketed), features six haunted houses, eight scare zones and live performances with “unrelenting frights and shocking surprises lurking around every corner” on select nights through Oct. 31. (SeaWorld’s family-friendly Spooktacular event features trick-or-treating included in park admission, a pumpkin patch and other family festivities.) Tickets are at seaworld.com/san-diego/events/howl-o-scream. Haunted house in Old Town: The historically significant Whaley House, which is billed as “America’s most haunted house,” holds various tours at its museum exploring the historic legacy, mystery and legends of the Whaley Family. The tours include Ghosts & Gravestones, Whaley House After Hours Paranormal Investigation and Whaley House Evening Guided Tour. For tickets, visit whaleyhousesandiego.com. Fright Night: The Halloween annual event is from 5 to 9 p.m. Oct. 30 in historic downtown and features a haunted house at the Avo Theater, trick-or-treating and a costume contest. Haunted house admission is $8; $5 for kids 10 and younger at The Avo Playhouse ticket box office, day of event. Visit discovervista.com/fright-night.

item.title: 13 best family-friendly safari lodges in Africa for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
In all this wondrous world, it’s hard to find an experience as fascinating for the entire family as an African safari, and staying in one of the best family-friendly safari lodges in Africa is crucial to a successful trip. This is where children’s storybooks come to life – not from behind fences or glass but with only the cleanest air possible between them and the animals. Fresh off a Kenyan safari that included my entire family, from my infant niece to my own two- and five-year-olds to my octogenarian mother, I’m reminded again that it’s not only the fantastical presence of towering giraffes, dazzling zebras, funny-looking rhinos, impressive elephants – though it’s undoubtedly their wrinkly babies who are the cutest animal around – and fearsome yet cuddly lions who make the magic. It’s the striking environment, the elements and all the questions that bubble to the surface as a result of simply being there. I was a safari nut before having children, having journeyed through seven African countries in search of spectacular wildlife, and I couldn’t wait to take my husband and our firstborn on their inaugural experience when she was not even a year old. Of course, I was under no disillusion that she would remember any of it. But babies actually make great safari-goers. Many love to bump around in a stroller or are lulled to sleep in a car, and the open-air Land Cruisers are a great combination of both. (Prepare to change diapers on a bench seat, and bring an air-tight bag for disposing of them, though!) When safari-ing with children, it’s always necessary to have a private vehicle and guide, and thus the timing of drives is generally flexible to work with little ones’ sleep times. Childcare is also often a part of the offering at the most family friendly safari lodges. On our first as a threesome, my husband and I opted to do a night drive sans baby, so I nursed and put her down before leaving; when we returned she was sleepy-eyed and tied to the babysitter’s back with a cloth, local style, having not slept a wink but spent most of the time playing with her sweet minder. The real fun starts once little ones can talk, or at least communicate what they’re seeing. I’ve found two to three years to be the most thrilling time where they are engaged and absolutely delighted by every single animal. As they get older and opinions form, it’s wildly entertaining. And our five year old hilariously now requests certain species as if she could order them off a menu, though she also savours the scavenger hunt-like search for them or the discovery of even the tiniest critter that, as only the best guides (often fathers or mothers themselves) can do, becomes something completely captivating. Yes, it’s one of the most adventurous things you could ever do as a family, but it’s also one of the most worthwhile – especially at one of the properties that embraces kids. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. item.title: Get ready, badge sales for Comic-Con 2027 happen in three weeks
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
Comic-Con fans beware, you have three weeks to prepare for the online sale of coveted badges for next year’s sure-to-sell-out show. Organizers of the annual gathering say purchasers will have an opportunity to buy badges for all four days of the convention, plus preview night. Open registration, as it is known, will begin at 9 a.m. Nov. 14, although a virtual waiting room will open at 7:30 a.m., allowing hopeful attendees plenty of time to arrive by the start of ticket sales. There is no advantage to arriving early. Next year’s convention will be held be held July 22-25, with preview night on Wednesday, July 21. Ticket prices range from $67 to $88 for each day of the convention, with discounts offered for teens ages 13 to 17 and for veterans and seniors. Children ages 12 and under are free with a paying adult. Organizers warn, as they do every year, that the demand far exceeds available badges, given the space limitations of San Diego’s downtown convention center. The massive pop culture gathering typically draws more than 135,000 attendees each year. “We know that purchasing a badge can be a challenge and we are constantly exploring options to improve your online registration experience,” Comic-Con organizers said. “We will continue to offer deeply discounted rates for juniors, seniors, and active-duty military, as well as one of the most generous free child badge policies in the comic convention industry.” To join the sale on Nov. 14, purchasers will need to log in to the member ID portal. But before that, aspiring attendees should ensure they have a valid ID by going to that site to verify their details are up to date. For new participants, they can create an account in advance of the sale at that same site. Comic-Con offers these additional tips to guarantee a smooth badge-buying experience: - Entry to the waiting room at any time does not ensure a registration session for purchasing entry to next year’s Comic-Con. - To avoid technical issues, use only one browser on a single device per person during the badge sale. Using multiple browsers or devices can disrupt your session. - The badge registration system is not formatted for iPads, tablets, or mobile devices. Although mobile devices can be used to purchase a badge, Comic-Con says it is unable to guarantee that the registration system will behave as expected using a mobile device. - If you are already logged in to your member ID account before the waiting room opens, click “Open Registration” from the top menu bar once the waiting room opens at 7:30 a.m. - If you are buying badges for others, you must have their member IDs and last names exactly as shown in their accounts. You can purchase badges for up to three people, including yourself. - Shortly after 9:00 a.m., groups will automatically begin moving from the waiting room to registration sessions in the order of the randomized queue. Only those selected for a registration session will have the opportunity to purchase badges. If you are moved from the waiting room to purchase badges, a timer will appear at the top of your page so you can keep track of how much time you have left during your 15-minute registration session. - Badges are offered as daily options only. There is a chance that the badges you’ve added to your cart will not be available by the time you process your order. - You will not be able to check out with a badge for Wednesday in your cart unless you are purchasing all four daily badge options (Thursday-Sunday). - Badge confirmations will be sent at a later date, once the refund deadline has passed.

item.title: I Deal With Chronic Back Pain. This Lightweight Gear Makes Backpacking Easier.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy How We Reported This: The author has chronic back pain, but she’s not ready to give up backpacking. Instead, she’s editing her kit to include lightweight backpacking gear, from her Mountain Hardwear Alakazam 45L pack to her Exped Ultra 6.5R sleeping pad, to make overnight trips more manageable and comfortable. A combination of old injuries, a couple car accidents, working most days at a desk, and stress I tend to carry in my body has left me with chronic upper back, neck, and shoulder pain. On my worst days, I can hardly turn my head from side to side, and a sharpness radiates from my shoulder blades to the base of my skull. Flare-ups like these can make the idea of shouldering a heavy backpack over many miles and sleeping on the ground sound like the death of me. Despite it all, I’ve never considered giving up backpacking (or my other outdoor hobbies) because of my back. Instead, as I’ve gotten older, more prone to injury, and less tolerant of pain, I’m paying closer attention to how much weight I’m carrying (and my posture). The ultralight lifestyle isn’t entirely for me—what do you mean my 500-page novel is discouraged?—but I’m taking a page out of the UL book and looking for lightweight backpacking gear that reduces backpacking’s impact on my body to make time on the trail more comfortable. As I’ve whittled down my backpacking kit, I’m aiming to drop my base weight from about 22 pounds to 15 without sacrificing support or comfort. That means swapping in lighter gear where I can and making room for a recovery tool to ease back pain after long days on the trail. My previous backpacking pack weighed close to 4 pounds. The Mountain Hardwear Alakazam 45L weighs just under 2 pounds but still has all the features I want in a backpacking pack, such as a sturdy and supportive aluminum frame. The frame attaches to the hip belt at the center back for even weight distribution, and the load lifters and GiddyUp Compression System help cinch the load. Weight savings come from the zipperless design—the roll-top opening is wide and easy to pack and unpack—and the waterproof ALUULA Graflyte V78 shell fabric. Unlike Dyneema, ALUULA bonds ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene fibers to a polymer film without adhesives, making it more resistant to delamination, abrasion, and tearing. A large front stash pocket and two oversized, dual-entry water bottle side pockets offer plenty of storage (though reaching behind my back for a bottle is awkward without taking off the pack or asking for help). For backpacking with back pain, I’ve found that the running vest-style straps keep the load close to my body and help distribute weight across my chest, rather than concentrating pressure on my shoulders. Because I usually backpack with a partner, I can split the weight of our shared gear between us. That means I don’t need the absolute lightest tent, cook set, or stove. Still, with a packed weight of 2 pounds 8 ounces, the semi-freestanding NEMO Hornet OSMO is impressively light even if I carried it solo. Split between two people, the tent’s weight comes to a little over a pound per person. The single hub makes for a quick setup, and the 27.7 square feet leaves just a little extra room for gear or a dog compared to roomier tents. The vestibule adds 7.1 square feet on each side, though. Peak height is 39 inches, which, for shorter people like myself, is plenty. My favorite feature is the overhead nightlight pockets for reading before bed. With a tent so light and compact, perhaps I have space for that 500-page novel after all. As if hiking with a loaded pack isn’t enough to aggravate my back, add in spending the night on the hard ground. But if you’re looking for the best sleeping pad for back pain, the Exped Ultra 6.5R is a standout contender. Earlier this year, Exped launched its lightest and warmest sleeping pad to date: the Ultra 6.5R. After a summer of testing it on backpacking and camping trips, I was surprised by how much cushioning it provided between my spine and the forest floor. Its 3.5 inches of loft help keep rocks and roots from becoming pressure points, while its 6.9 R-value makes it suitable for year-round use, even when temperatures dip below freezing. Despite all that padding and insulation, the regular rectangular version weighs just over a pound and packs down small. Raised side rails help keep me centered on the mat, too, so I’m less likely to roll off in the middle of the night. It won’t eliminate my back pain, but having a more supportive place to lie down makes waking up ready to hike again that much easier. I have friends who use their extra clothes in a stuff sack as a pillow, and I’ve tried it too. But I always wake up with a crick in my neck that derails the day and regret not bringing a real pillow. These days, lightweight backpacking pillows weigh so little that saving a few ounces hardly seems worth the trade-off. I like a pillow with a microfiber exterior that doesn’t stick to my face, and the Exped Down Pillow is small and light enough at 5.3 ounces (size medium) to feel negligible in my pack. Filled with air, it’s easy to adjust the firmness to tuck between my shoulder and chin, and perfectly cradle my head. No headaches to start the day with this companion. On a hut-to-hut run in New Hampshire’s White Mountains several years ago, a fellow runner packed a lacrosse ball to roll out tight muscles. I thought he was ridiculous for carrying the extra weight—until the last evening, when I borrowed it for my tight IT bands and knotty back. Now, I rarely head into the backcountry without some kind of recovery tool. I’ve used these silicone cups weekly since 2019, and I’ve even packed one single cup along on backpacking trips. At 1.3 ounces, it’s 4 ounces lighter than a lacrosse ball. Sport cups use suction to lift the skin and underlying superficial tissue, potentially increasing local blood flow and temporarily relieving pain. Evidence for cupping’s effectiveness is limited, but I’ve found it provides short-term relief at the end of a long day. Once I get to my campsite, I apply a CBD balm or oil to the sore area and suction one of these cups to the spot for 5 to 15 minutes. I can feel my knots fade in real time.
